Assets.Functionality: Machine software interrupt input that signals a software-generated interrupt to the CPU's machine-level interrupt logic and is folded into the irq_machine vector.
Assets.Justification: Manipulation or persistent assertion of this interrupt input can prevent forward progress of normal software (interrupt storms or unwanted context switches), effectively causing denial-of-service. Because it controls interrupt-driven flow rather than carrying secret data or configuration, availability is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Machine external interrupt input that signals external interrupt requests to the CPU's machine-level interrupt handling and is combined into irq_machine.
Assets.Justification: An attacker who can assert or withhold this input can induce spurious interrupts or block expected external interrupts, disrupting normal operation and causing denial-of-service. The primary risk is interruption/denial of normal execution, so availability is the dominant objective.

Assets.Functionality: Internal 3-bit vector combining mti_i, mei_i and msi_i used by the control unit to represent machine-level interrupts.
Assets.Justification: irq_machine is the synthesized internal interrupt representation used by the control path; if this signal is tampered with it can enable persistent interrupts or mask them, causing denial-of-service or stalled execution. It is the internal availability-critical representation of external interrupt inputs.

Assets.Functionality: Machine timer interrupt input used to notify the control unit of timer-based events (mti) which drive timer interrupts and scheduling decisions.
Assets.Justification: Corrupting or spamming the timer interrupt can prevent timely progress of time-sensitive tasks or create continual interruptions, impairing system availability. The signal affects control flow and liveness rather than confidentiality or integrity of stored data.

Assets.Functionality: 16-bit vector of custom fast/low-latency interrupt inputs providing multiple fast interrupt sources to the CPU.
Assets.Justification: If an attacker can assert or hold these fast interrupt lines, they can forcibly preempt or stall normal execution, causing denial-of-service or livelock. Because the vector primarily affects control flow and responsiveness, availability is the key objective.

Assets.Functionality: Debug halt request input used to request the CPU to enter or handle debug/halt conditions from the debug subsystem.
Assets.Justification: This signal can directly stop or park CPU execution when asserted, providing an easy way for an attacker or misconfigured integrator to deny service to the system. The principal risk is halting normal operation, so availability is dominant.

Assets.Functionality: Input that signals the CPU when an external memory synchronization operation has completed, used to resume or finalize memory-related actions.
Assets.Justification: If this synchronization signal is not asserted or is manipulated, memory synchronization sequences cannot complete and the CPU may stall or fail to progress, causing denial-of-service. The main impact is operational liveness rather than confidentiality or integrity.

Assets.Asset Name: Load Data Output (Load/Store Unit Read Data)
Assets.Functionality: Data returned from the Load/Store Unit after a memory access and used as a write-back source into the register file.
Assets.Justification: lsu_rdata can carry sensitive data (e.g., secret keys or confidential memory contents) fetched from memory; unauthorized observation or exposure of this signal would leak secrets. Given the CPU's support for cryptographic extensions and that loads can return secret material, confidentiality is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Primary ALU result used as a write-back source to the register file and by downstream units for further computation.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of the ALU result will propagate incorrect data into the register file and subsequent computations, compromising correctness and possibly safety/ security properties. Because alu_res directly affects computational correctness/ state, integrity is the dominant objective.

Assets.Functionality: Address/result bus produced by the ALU used as the effective memory access address input to the LSU and as input to PMP/address checks.
Assets.Justification: If alu_add is modified or corrupted, memory accesses (loads/stores) will target incorrect addresses, leading to data corruption or privileged-data disclosure. Because it directly controls which memory locations are accessed, protecting its integrity is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Represents the effective address used for the most recent load/store and is provided to PMP and for debugging/diagnostic purposes.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with lsu_mar changes the effective memory address of data operations, which can corrupt memory or cause unintended side-effects. The primary impact is incorrect memory accesses, so integrity protection is required.

Assets.Asset Name: Register File Write Data Multiplexer Output
Assets.Functionality: Multiplexed write-back data fed into the register file (from ALU, LSU, CSR read data, or return PC) and thus determines what values get written to registers.
Assets.Justification: If rf_wdata is corrupted an attacker can inject arbitrary values into registers, changing program state and control/data flow. Because it determines register contents for future instructions, its integrity is essential.

Assets.Functionality: CSR read-data output produced by the control unit for CSR read instructions and selectable as a write-back source into the register file.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of CSR read data can lead to incorrect configuration or misreporting of system status and can change privileged behavior when written back. The main risk is incorrect control/configuration state, so integrity is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Flow-control signal from the LSU indicating the CPU must wait for an ongoing data bus access to complete; used by the control unit to stall instruction execution.
Assets.Justification: If lsu_wait is asserted permanently or manipulated, the CPU will stall and forward progress stops, causing denial-of-service. Because it controls execution liveness, availability is the primary objective.

Assets.Functionality: Flag asserted by the PMP on permission violations to signal the control unit and LSU about PMP access faults for exception handling or blocking accesses.
Assets.Justification: If pmp_fault is incorrectly asserted or manipulated at integration, it will block memory accesses and trigger exceptions, preventing normal operation. The primary impact is denying memory access/operation, therefore availability is the chief concern.

Assets.Functionality: Primary source operand 1 supplied from the register file and used by the comparator, adder/subtractor, logic operations and various co-processor units as an ALU input.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or malicious modification of rs1_i directly changes arithmetic/logic results, comparison outcomes and co-processor inputs, which can produce incorrect program behaviour or corrupt computed addresses/data. As an input operand, its integrity is critical to correct CPU operation.

Assets.Functionality: Primary source operand 2 supplied from the register file and used by the adder/subtractor, comparator, shift/multiply units and other co-processors as the second ALU input.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with rs2_i can change ALU computations, address calculations, and co-processor computations, leading to incorrect results or unintended memory accesses. Because many ALU operations depend on rs2_i, its integrity is essential for correct execution.

Assets.Functionality: Optional third source operand provided to co-processors (notably the FPU and CFU) for operations that require a third input (e.g., R4-type or fused FP ops).
Assets.Justification: rs3_i is used by FPU/CFU/custom operations; if altered, multi-operand co-processor operations will produce incorrect results or corrupt state. Maintaining correct rs3_i values is therefore an integrity requirement for co-processor correctness.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level ALU result output that multiplexes adder, comparator/slti result, co-processor results and logical operations based on control signals; this result is written back/observed by the rest of the CPU.
Assets.Justification: res_o is the principal data produced by the ALU; corrupting this output leads to incorrect computation results and program semantics. Ensuring res_o integrity prevents incorrect data propagation throughout the CPU.

Assets.Functionality: Direct XLEN-bit lower result from the adder/subtractor core used for address computations and other add/sub operations.
Assets.Justification: add_o is typically used for address generation; if its value is corrupted, memory accesses can be mis-directed or cause data corruption. Protecting add_o integrity prevents incorrect memory accesses and maintains system correctness.

Assets.Functionality: Comparator status output (equal and less-than flags) used for conditional branches and provided as input to conditional/bit-manipulation co-ops.
Assets.Justification: If cmp_o is modified or spoofed, branch/conditional decisions become incorrect causing control-flow hijacks or logic errors. The integrity of cmp_o is therefore critical for correct program flow.

Assets.Functionality: CSR read-back output that forwards CSR data from co-processor CSR proxies (FPU/CFU) when those CSRs are accessed.
Assets.Justification: csr_o exposes read-back values from co-processor CSRs; if those CSRs contain sensitive state or cryptographic-related data (possible via optional co-processors/custom functions), csr_o can leak that information. Therefore confidentiality of csr_o is important to prevent disclosure of sensitive internal data.

Assets.Functionality: CSR read-back data proxy for the FPU; driven to zero unless the FPU CSR block is being accessed, then forwarded to csr_o.
Assets.Justification: csr_rdata_fpu can carry internal FPU/co-processor register values to csr_o; if those registers include sensitive or implementation-specific state (or if optional co-processors expose secret-like values), this signal can disclose that data. Protecting confidentiality of csr_rdata_fpu prevents unintended leakage via CSR readbacks.

Assets.Functionality: Internal adder/subtractor result (with extra MSB) that feeds slt, add outputs and the add_o address result.
Assets.Justification: addsub_res is the internal source for addresses, add_o, and some status bits; if this internal value is corrupted, multiple externally visible outputs (addresses, slt flags) become incorrect. Thus the integrity of addsub_res is central to correct ALU behavior.

Assets.Functionality: OR/merge of individual co-processor result buses that is selected into res_o when co-processor output is the active ALU result source.
Assets.Justification: cp_res supplies co-processor outputs to res_o; tampering with cp_res causes incorrect ALU outputs for co-processor instructions and may corrupt program execution. Maintaining cp_res integrity preserves correctness of multi-cycle/co-processor operations.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level signal asserted when any multi-cycle co-processor indicates completion (set one cycle before the corresponding data is valid); used by the CPU to proceed after long-running ALU co-operations.
Assets.Justification: If done_o is suppressed or not asserted correctly an integrating master may never observe co-processor completion and stall or timeout, causing denial-of-service of co-processor operations. Availability of this strobe is therefore critical to maintain forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Vector of valid/done strobes (one bit per co-processor) indicating a co-processor will produce valid output next cycle; used to generate the done_o signal.
Assets.Justification: If cp_valid bits are withheld or manipulated to never assert, the system will not receive completion notifications (done_o) and co-processor results will effectively be unavailable, causing stalls or denial-of-service. Ensuring correct cp_valid behavior is therefore an availability requirement.

Assets.Functionality: Input that signals a physical memory protection (PMP) fault on instruction fetch/execute, which the trap controller latches as an instruction access/execute fault and may trigger a trap/exception.
Assets.Justification: If pmp_fault_i is asserted (or spoofed) at the integration level, the CPU will treat the current instruction fetch as a fault and start trap handling, preventing normal execution. An attacker or faulty integration that can force this line can repeatedly trigger traps or prevent forward progress, causing a denial-of-service on the CPU.

Assets.Functionality: Input handshake indicating completion of multi-cycle ALU/CFU/FPU operations; the execute FSM uses it to resume execution and perform register-file write-back for those operations.
Assets.Justification: If alu_cp_done_i is manipulated (asserted early or suppressed), the control FSM can incorrectly proceed to write-back or may wait indefinitely; early/spurious assertion can cause wrong results to be committed, corrupting register-file state and program semantics. Therefore this signal is critical to preserving correct computation integrity.

Assets.Functionality: External single-bit input used to request a debug-mode halt entry (if debug is enabled); it is treated as an async halt trigger and routed into debug-entry logic.
Assets.Justification: An adversary or misintegration asserting irq_dbg_i can force or repeatedly request halt/debug entry, preventing normal program execution and causing a denial-of-service. Because its dominant effect is to stop or pause the CPU, availability is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit input indicating the LSU has an outstanding memory transaction and that the execute FSM should wait in EX_MEM_RSP until completion.
Assets.Justification: If lsu_wait_i is held asserted by a compromised integrator or faulty subsystem, the execute FSM will stall waiting for memory responses and may never progress, resulting in a denial-of-service. Conversely, spuriously deasserting it can cause premature progression but the dominant risk at integration is DoS by driving it high.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates completion of memory synchronization operations; used to update exe_engine.msync (and combined with ctrl.lsu_fence) and to let the EX_FENCE state progress when synchronization completes.
Assets.Justification: If mem_sync_i is not asserted when required (or prevented), fence operations will not complete and the CPU may stall or remain in a fence waiting state, causing a denial-of-service for memory-ordered operations. Thus tampering with this line primarily impacts availability of correct execution.

Assets.Functionality: Internal handshake asserted to acknowledge that an instruction word supplied by the front-end is being consumed by the backend (backend-to-frontend handshake).
Assets.Justification: if_ack controls the handshake protocol with the front-end; if it is prevented from asserting (or asserted incorrectly by corrupted logic), instruction transfer and dispatch can be disrupted, leading to instruction fetch stalls or lost synchrony and therefore denial-of-service. At integration level, manipulation of the handshake affects ability to fetch/dispatch instructions.

Assets.Functionality: Internal control signal used to reset/flush the instruction fetch front-end on branches, restarts or trap events; forwarded to the front-end via the control bus.
Assets.Justification: If if_reset is toggled maliciously or incorrectly, the front-end can be repeatedly reset or held in reset, preventing instruction fetch and halting execution (DoS). Because it gates the front-end progress, integrity impact is secondary to the availability impact.

Assets.Functionality: Captures fault-specific information (e.g., faulting address for load/store exceptions) on trap entry for diagnostic/handler use.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of mtval hides or falsifies the faulting address or instruction, impeding correct diagnosis and recovery of memory faults. Handlers rely on mtval integrity to react correctly to faults.

Assets.Functionality: Combinatorial flag set when the decoded instruction is illegal or unsupported; used to raise illegal-instruction exceptions and feed trap logic.
Assets.Justification: If illegal_cmd is forced high (or inputs that set it are manipulated), the CPU will raise an illegal-instruction trap and can be prevented from executing intended instructions, resulting in denial-of-service. While it relates to correctness, the primary risk at integration is blocking normal execution.

Assets.Asset Name: CSR write enable and write control
Assets.Functionality: Indicates and controls when a CSR write should occur (drives updates to the CSR register set). Writes are gated by csr.we and related checks (illegal-instr, privilege).
Assets.Justification: If CSR write control is corrupted, privileged CSRs may be written or blocked unexpectedly, altering configuration and control state. Protecting csr.we integrity prevents unauthorized or spurious modification of critical registers.

Assets.Functionality: Vector input of standard RISC-V machine interrupts (MSI, MEI, MTI) that are sampled into the interrupt-pending buffer and participate in priority/irq firing logic.
Assets.Justification: Machine-level interrupts drive forward progress (timer tick, external events, and software interrupts). If these lines are dropped, delayed, or incorrectly masked, irq_pnd/irq_buf will not set and irq_fire will not trigger despite mie/mstatus enabling, leading to missed trap entries, stalled scheduling, and system hang—directly degrading availability.

Assets.Functionality: Vector input of NEORV32-specific fast interrupts latched into irq-pending/buffer and used for fast interrupt trap entries.
Assets.Justification: Fast interrupts serve latency-sensitive servicing; corruption or loss prevents env_enter/irq_fire from initiating the handler (even when mie_firq is set), causing missed deadlines, peripheral overruns, and prolonged service starvation—conditions that reduce overall system availability.

Assets.Functionality: Internal register indicating whether the CPU is currently in debug-mode (online) and gating debug-specific behavior (e.g., privilege handling, stopping counters, gating interrupts).
Assets.Justification: If debug_ctrl.run is forced or stuck in the debug state, the CPU operates in debug-mode semantics and may halt or prevent normal execution causing denial-of-service. Because debug mode changes execution flow and can stop normal operation, availability is the main security effect.

Assets.Functionality: Internal sticky flag that marks when a hardware trigger (address match) has fired; used to generate breakpoint/ebreak or debug-entry and presented via trigger CSR read-back.
Assets.Justification: If the hwtrig_fired status is set (or prevented from being cleared), it will cause or report breakpoint-like conditions that can trigger traps or debug entries, interrupting normal execution. Manipulation can be used to induce repeated trap entries or prevent clearing of a fired trigger, leading to denial-of-service.

Assets.Functionality: Global CSR read-data output that presents the selected CSR read-back value by OR-ing cycle_rd, time_rd, instret_rd and hpm_rd into the module's CSR read result.
Assets.Justification: rdata_o is the primary read-back interface for all counter CSRs; if it is blocked, driven incorrectly, or suppressed, software and integrators cannot obtain any counter values, effectively denying the use of the counters. This prevents the monitoring/observability function of the IP (DoS on readback) and therefore is an availability-critical asset.

Assets.Functionality: Per-counter increment enable bits computed by the cnt_control process; each bit enables incrementing its corresponding counter when its event fires and counting is not halted or in debug.
Assets.Justification: cnt_en gates whether counters actually increment on events; if cnt_en bits are held low or otherwise disabled, the counters will cease to update and monitoring is effectively denied. Because this directly prevents the counters from performing their intended runtime function, it is an availability-critical asset.

Assets.Functionality: 16-bit vector of write-enable strobes for counter CSRs: asserted when a counter access is decoded (cnt_acc), the respective sel bit is set, and csr_we is active; used to load counter sub-words from CSR writes.
Assets.Justification: cnt_we controls which counters accept CSR writes; unauthorized assertion or manipulation of cnt_we allows injecting or corrupting counter values via writes, undermining the correctness of counter state. Since it enables modification of sensitive measurement state, this signal is integrity-critical.

Assets.Functionality: 16-bit vector of write-enable strobes for mhpmeventx CSRs (HPM configuration): asserted when a config access is decoded (cfg_acc), the respective sel bit is set, and csr_we is active; used to update hpmevent registers.
Assets.Justification: cfg_we gates writes to the hpmevent configuration registers; if an attacker can assert or tamper with cfg_we they can change which events HPM counters track, corrupting monitoring semantics. Because cfg_we enables modification of configuration that determines what gets counted, it is an integrity-critical asset.

Assets.Functionality: Array of 12-bit registers holding each HPM's mhpmeventx configuration; they select which events increment the associated HPM counters and are written via cfg_we when software writes the corresponding CSR.
Assets.Justification: hpmevent entries directly determine which events increment each HPM counter; unauthorized modification changes monitored events and corrupts the meaning and trustworthiness of HPM measurements. Therefore these configuration registers are integrity-critical assets.

Assets.Asset Name: Hardware Performance Monitor Counters read values
Assets.Functionality: Array of HPM counter read-back values (m[h]pmcnt3..m[h]pmcntN) that hold the current counts of selected hardware events and contribute to the aggregated HPM read-back logic.
Assets.Justification: Software depends on these values to reflect true event counts; if gating or addressing is subverted (e.g., via sel, cnt_acc/cfg_acc, or spurious cnt_we/cfg_we), reads can be forged or stale, corrupting diagnostics and masking anomalous activity—violating integrity.

Assets.Functionality: One-hot vector derived from CSR address low bits that selects which indexed counter or mhpmevent entry is targeted by the current CSR access.
Assets.Justification: This decode steers which register is read or written; any corruption of sel can redirect accesses to the wrong index, causing unintended modification or spoofed observations of counters/configuration and thereby compromising data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 16-bit vector of read-enable strobes for counter CSRs: asserted when a counter access is decoded (cnt_acc), the respective sel bit is set, and csr_re is active; used by submodules to present counter values on their rdata_o.
Assets.Justification: cnt_re controls whether a counter's value is made available for readback; if cnt_re bits are suppressed or blocked, the corresponding counter values cannot be observed via CSR reads, denying read access to those counters. This is a denial-of-service on the module's readback capability and therefore an availability-critical asset.

Assets.Functionality: Low-word register storing the lower lo_width_c bits of a generic counter instance; updated either by CSR write (when sel_i='0' and we_i) or by increment logic on events.
Assets.Justification: lo_q holds the persistent counter value for the low sub-word; unauthorized writes or corruption change the counter result and corrupt measurement data. Because these registers are the canonical storage of counter values, their integrity is critical.

Assets.Functionality: High-word register storing the upper hi_width_c bits of a generic counter instance (for counters wider than XLEN); updated by CSR write when sel_i='1' or incremented by the staged carry from the low word.
Assets.Justification: hi_q forms the upper portion of wide counters and is required to maintain correct extended counter values; corruption or unauthorized writes to hi_q will produce incorrect combined counter values. Thus hi_q is an integrity-critical asset for correct counter functionality.

Assets.Functionality: Read-enable input that gates presenting the selected counter sub-word on the rdata_o output when asserted; otherwise the submodule outputs zeros.
Assets.Justification: re_i controls whether valid counter data is placed on rdata_o; if it is stuck low or corrupted, reads return zeros and software loses visibility into counter progress, causing polling loops and services that depend on these values to stall. Ensuring re_i operates correctly preserves system liveness and prevents denial-of-service via suppressed reads.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit increment input to the generic counter that causes the low-word to be incremented on the next clock when asserted, propagating carry to the high-word if applicable.
Assets.Justification: inc_i is the trigger for forward progress of the counter; if it is blocked or stuck low, the counter freezes and any time/event-based mechanisms relying on it cannot progress, leading to denial-of-service. Spurious assertion can also force unintended advancements/overflows, disrupting liveness guarantees and service continuity.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit primary operand input that is buffered into rs1_reg and used by most bit-manipulation operations (shifts/rotates, popcount, byte ops, rev8, clmul LHS, etc.).
Assets.Justification: If rs1_i or its buffered copy (rs1_reg) is corrupted or tampered, every downstream computation that depends on it (shifters, clmul, adders, and derived results such as res_int/res_out) becomes incorrect and can be written back to architectural state, causing silent state corruption and violating computational correctness.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit secondary operand input buffered into rs2_reg and used for operations such as shifted-add, packing, logical-negate ops, and carry-less multiplication (RHS).
Assets.Justification: Integrity of rs2_i (and rs2_reg) is essential because it directly determines arithmetic, logical, and clmul outcomes; any manipulation results in incorrect res_int/res_out values that propagate to write-back and corrupt architectural state.

Assets.Functionality: Result output vector driven by the selected operation and presented on the rising clock when the coprocessor signals the result is valid; consumed by the core/register file or next-stage logic.
Assets.Justification: The res_o port is the module's externally-observable output and therefore can leak processed data or intermediate values. The RTL and spec show support for cryptography-related operations (Zbkb/Zbkc/CLMUL), so results produced on res_o can carry secret/cryptographic material and must be protected from unauthorized observation.

Assets.Functionality: Internal buffered copy of the external operand rs1_i used as the primary input for virtually all bit-manipulation operations (shifts, rotates, logical ops, zip/pack, clmul, etc.).
Assets.Justification: rs1_reg holds operand data inside the co-processor and is used directly by many operations including those intended for cryptographic purposes (e.g., carry-less multiply). If the module processes secret keys or plaintext, rs1_reg would contain sensitive material that could be leaked via outputs or side-channels, so it is confidentiality-critical.

Assets.Functionality: Internal buffered copy of the external operand rs2_i used as the second operand for operations such as logic-with-negate, shifted-add, pack, and carry-less multiplication.
Assets.Justification: Like rs1_reg, rs2_reg stores operand data that may be cryptographic secrets when the bit-manipulation extension is used for crypto-related operations. Exposure of rs2_reg contents (or its propagated results) would leak sensitive data, so it is confidentiality-critical.

Assets.Functionality: Index-sized input that controls shift/rotate distance, single-bit selection (one_hot generator), and is sampled into sha_reg for operations requiring a bit index or rotation amount.
Assets.Justification: shamt_i influences which bits are set/cleared/extracted and how data is rotated or shifted (affecting one_hot_res, shifter behavior, bs_shift). An integrity compromise of shamt_i (or its buffered sha_reg) can intentionally alter operation results, corrupt data-flow, or cause incorrect selection of bits, so it is integrity-critical.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit comparator status input sampled into less_reg and used by selection logic (e.g., MIN/MAX instructions) to decide which operand to forward as the result.
Assets.Justification: cmp_i (and buffered less_reg) controls the min/max selection logic; if corrupted an attacker can force selection of the wrong operand, altering outputs and corrupting program semantics. Because it directly changes which data is returned, the comparator input is an integrity-critical asset.

Assets.Functionality: Vector of decoded command flags (one bit per supported operation) that identifies which specific bit-manipulation operation should be executed and gates generation of res_out entries.
Assets.Justification: cmd selects the operation performed by the module; if the decoded command bits are tampered with, the module can perform an unintended operation (e.g., expose different computation or corrupt data). Maintaining the integrity of cmd is therefore essential to ensure correct and authorized behavior.

Assets.Functionality: External 1-bit output indicating that res_o holds a valid result; consumers use it to accept/consume the result produced by the co-processor.
Assets.Justification: valid_o is the module's external readiness/handshake signal. If valid_o is withheld or stuck low an integrator or downstream logic cannot retrieve results even though they exist, producing a denial-of-service for the co-processor's functionality, so it is availability-critical.

Assets.Functionality: FSM state (S_IDLE, S_START, S_BUSY) that manages operation start, multi-cycle operation progression, and completion. It controls starting iterative cores, issuing valid, and returning to idle.
Assets.Justification: ctrl_state governs whether operations are started, run and complete. If the FSM is corrupted or stuck in a non-progressing state the module cannot complete operations or assert valid, preventing normal operation and causing a denial-of-service; hence it is availability-critical.

Assets.Functionality: Array of four 32-bit words used to store the XTEA round/key words; written via CSR writes and read asynchronously for round computations.
Assets.Justification: key_mem holds the secret cryptographic key material used by the XTEA algorithm. If key_mem is exposed or read out by an integrator or attacker, the confidentiality of all encryption/decryption operations is broken.

Assets.Asset Name: CSR Write Data (CSR -> key write payload)
Assets.Functionality: 32-bit data value supplied during a CSR write; when csr_we_i is asserted it is synchronously written into key_mem at the index given by csr_addr_i.
Assets.Justification: csr_wdata_i contains the new key word or CSR configuration written into key_mem; tampering or erroneous values on this port directly corrupt the stored key/configuration and therefore compromise operational integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit index selecting which key_mem element (0..3) is targeted by a CSR write or read access.
Assets.Justification: csr_addr_i controls which key word is modified or read. Corrupting this index can cause writes/reads to target wrong key words, corrupting the key or producing incorrect behavior; integrity of this selector is therefore critical.

Assets.Functionality: Single-cycle strobe indicating a valid CSR write; when high on a clock edge causes csr_wdata_i to be written into key_mem[csr_addr_i].
Assets.Justification: csr_we_i gates writes into the key storage. An attacker or compromised master toggling csr_we_i at the wrong time (or forging writes) can corrupt key material or configuration, undermining correctness and cryptographic integrity.

Assets.Asset Name: CSR Read Data Output (key/status leak path)
Assets.Functionality: Asynchronous 32-bit read port driven with the contents of key_mem indexed by csr_addr_i; used by the CPU to read CFU CSRs.
Assets.Justification: csr_rdata_o directly outputs the contents of key_mem to the CPU on CSR reads; therefore it is a clear channel by which secret key words can be leaked to software or an adversary with read access, making it a confidentiality-critical interface.

Assets.Functionality: 3-bit selector from the instruction word that selects the CFU operation (init / encrypt v0/v1 / decrypt v0/v1) and controls operand/round-key handling.
Assets.Justification: funct3_i selects the CFU operation mode (including initialization vs. encrypt/decrypt). If corrupted, the CFU can run unintended modes (e.g., skip initialization or use wrong arithmetic), altering results and breaking functional integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit source register 1 supplied by the CPU and buffered into xtea.opa on operation start; used as one of the two XTEA data operands.
Assets.Justification: rs1_i supplies operand data and can also initialize the round-key buffer; if rs1_i is maliciously altered or corrupted, the CFU will produce incorrect or manipulated cryptographic results, compromising computation integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit source register 2 supplied by the CPU and buffered into xtea.opb on operation start; used as the second XTEA data operand.
Assets.Justification: rs2_i is the second operand for XTEA rounds; tampering with rs2_i corrupts the computation and yields incorrect encryption/decryption outputs, so protecting its integrity is essential.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit internal round-key buffer that is initialized or incremented/decremented by the XTEA delta during processing and whose bits index key_mem for selecting the round key word.
Assets.Justification: xtea.sum controls which key word is used and how round keys evolve; corruption of this internal register (e.g., via fault or integration-level manipulation) will change key selection and arithmetic, destroying correctness and intended cryptographic behavior.

Assets.Asset Name: Buffered Operand Register opa (internal operand buffer)
Assets.Functionality: Internal 32-bit register that buffers rs1_i as one operand for timing and for use in the XTEA computation pipeline.
Assets.Justification: xtea.opa stores an operand that may be secret while the cryptographic operation is in progress; internal exposure of this buffer would leak sensitive plaintext/ciphertext, so it is confidentiality-critical.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle strobe that triggers/buffers a new CFU operation when asserted (and rtype_i indicates the correct instruction format).
Assets.Justification: start_i is the entry trigger for CFU operations; if an attacker or faulty integration prevents start_i from being asserted (or drops the strobe), CFU operations cannot be initiated, producing a denial-of-service on the accelerator functionality.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates the CPU is waiting for the CFU / that an operation is in progress; per interface spec the CFU should cease processing when this deasserts.
Assets.Justification: active_i controls whether multi-cycle processing is expected; if active_i is de-asserted prematurely (or held inactive), the CFU must cease/reset operations or the CPU will not accept results, causing aborted operations or denial-of-service of CFU functions.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit operation result driven to the CPU when an operation completes (written into the CPU register file).
Assets.Justification: result_o conveys processed data (ciphertext or plaintext) from the CFU to the CPU; this output can leak sensitive plaintext or intermediate secrets derived from the key if exposed, so confidentiality is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Single-cycle strobe asserting that result_o is valid; the CPU samples this to accept the CFU result (for multi-cycle operations it follows xtea.done).
Assets.Justification: valid_o is the signal that enables the CPU to accept and write back the CFU result; if valid_o is not asserted (or suppressed) the CPU will time out or raise an exception, preventing use of the CFU result and effectively denying service.

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 1 (XLEN bits). When the unit is triggered and the evaluated condition is true, this value is forwarded to res_o on the clock edge.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or unauthorized modification of rs1_i directly changes the value produced by the conditional move, causing incorrect architectural state or computation results. Because rs1_i is the primary data forwarded by the unit, its integrity is critical to correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 2 (XLEN bits). Compared against zero to form the zero/non-zero condition that determines whether rs1_i is forwarded to res_o.
Assets.Justification: Tampering rs2_i changes the evaluated condition (zero vs non-zero) and therefore can enable or disable forwarding of rs1_i incorrectly, altering control flow or data outputs. As a control-like input that gates result selection, its integrity is essential.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit operation result. Driven with rs1_i when a valid conditional instruction is recognized and the condition is true; otherwise driven to zero.
Assets.Justification: If res_o is unavailable (e.g., blocked or not propagated to consumers), downstream pipeline stages or units will not receive the result, causing stalls or denial-of-service of the operation. Ensuring res_o is delivered is required for correct forward progress of the CPU.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit data-output-valid signal indicating that the module recognized the targeted co-processor conditional instruction (driven from valid_cmd) and that res_o is meaningful.
Assets.Justification: If valid_o is suppressed or unavailable, consumers will ignore res_o even when a correct result exists, effectively producing a denial-of-service. valid_o directly gates use of the result so its availability is necessary for normal operation.

Assets.Functionality: Comparator flag that is '1' when rs2_i equals zero; used as part of the condition evaluation to decide zero vs non-zero tests.
Assets.Justification: Tampering rs2_zero alters the evaluated condition used to permit forwarding of rs1_i, leading to incorrect enable/disable decisions for the conditional move. Since it participates in the condition computation, its integrity is required for correct conditional behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Final evaluated condition (rs2_zero xnor ctrl_i.ir_funct3(1)) determining whether the conditional test succeeded; when true together with valid_cmd it enables passing rs1 to res_o on the next clock.
Assets.Justification: If condition is corrupted, the module will incorrectly enable or disable forwarding of rs1_i, causing wrong results or unintended data flow. As the ultimate control used to gate the result, maintaining its integrity is critical to correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 1 supplied to the crypto co-processor and latched into internal rs1 when a crypto instruction is valid; used as primary data input for permutations, hash, AES/SM4 and other operations.
Assets.Justification: rs1_i can hold plaintexts, keys, or other secret intermediates for the crypto unit; exposure via buses, debug, or side channels would disclose sensitive information, so its value must remain confidential.

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 2 supplied to the crypto co-processor and latched into internal rs2 when a crypto instruction is valid; used as secondary data, byte/nibble selectors, and S-box indices.
Assets.Justification: rs2_i often carries secret-dependent selectors or S-box indices; revealing it can leak key-dependent patterns and aid key recovery, so confidentiality of this operand is essential.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit S-box output read from SM4 ROM and latched each clock; zero-extended to sm4.so2 and used to compute the SM4 round or key-schedule word.
Assets.Justification: The S-box output is a key-dependent intermediate of SM4; observing or inferring this byte enables differential or correlation attacks, so it must remain internal and confidential.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered copy of the instruction's 12-bit funct field used to select the specific crypto sub-function, control internal multiplexers, byte-rotation, mix-steps and out_sel.
Assets.Justification: funct12 governs cryptographic subfunction selection and internal routing; if altered, the unit can execute the wrong operation or sequence, producing incorrect results, so its integrity must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered copy of the instruction's 3-bit funct3 field used by decode/operation selection (e.g., xperm byte/nibble choice) and other selection logic.
Assets.Justification: funct3 participates in decode and variant selection; corruption misroutes control and yields incorrect function choice, so strong integrity of this field is required.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle-wide internal pulse asserted when an operation is finished; used to drive valid_o and to qualify/reserve res_o for a single cycle.
Assets.Justification: The one-cycle completion pulse drives the result handshake; if suppressed, stretched, or duplicated, instructions cannot retire reliably and the pipeline can stall, so it is critical for availability.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit output driven one cycle when an operation completes; conveys the selected functional-unit result back to the core/register file.
Assets.Justification: res_o delivers the computed result to the core; if it is withheld or not presented in time, dependent instructions cannot proceed and system progress halts, making its timely availability essential.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle valid pulse indicating res_o contains a completed operation result; driven from internal done signal to signal readiness to the integrating CPU.
Assets.Justification: valid_o signals that res_o is ready; missing or spurious assertions cause stalls or lost results, directly impacting forward progress, so this indicator is availability-critical.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the active floating-point rounding mode (3 bits) used by the normalizer and conversion units to decide how results are rounded for all FP operations.
Assets.Justification: If csr_frm is modified (e.g., via CSR writes) an attacker or faulty integration could change rounding semantics, producing incorrect or unexpected numeric results across the system. Maintaining integrity of the rounding mode is essential because it directly alters arithmetic outcomes and software-visible behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Accumulated 5-bit FPU exception flags (NV, DZ, OF, UF, NX) that are read/written via CSR accesses and auto-accumulated from fflags produced by operations.
Assets.Justification: Corrupting csr_fflags can hide or fabricate exception conditions (e.g., invalid operation or inexact) which influence software decisions (error handling, control flow). Preserving integrity of the flags is necessary to ensure correct exception reporting and subsequent behavior by software.

Assets.Functionality: Input control that gates write access to FPU CSRs (frm/fflags/fcsr); when asserted allows CSR updates from csr_wdata_i to internal CSR registers.
Assets.Justification: If csr_we_i is asserted incorrectly or manipulated, an attacker could cause unauthorized writes to csr_frm or csr_fflags, changing rounding modes or flags and thereby corrupting computation results or exception state. Protecting the integrity of this control prevents unauthorized modification of critical FPU control state.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit input that selects which FPU CSR (fflags, frm or fcsr) is targeted for CSR read/write operations.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with csr_addr_i can redirect CSR writes/reads to the wrong internal register (e.g., overwrite frm instead of fflags), corrupting control/state and causing incorrect FP behavior or misleading status. Ensuring correctness of the selected CSR protects internal control data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit input carrying the first operand (integer-encoded single-precision float) from the CPU register file used by classifier, arithmetic, compare and conversion units.
Assets.Justification: If rs1_i is corrupted at integration (malicious bus, tampered memory/register file) the FPU will consume wrong operand data producing incorrect results and potentially causing safety- or correctness-critical failures. Protecting operand integrity is fundamental to correct computation.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the encoded operation class (e.g., add/sub, mul, compare, convert) selected at issue and used to route results through the core.
Assets.Justification: Changing the selected function will cause the FPU to perform a different operation than intended, corrupting computations; keeping funct_ff correct is essential to preserve functional integrity of the processor pipeline.

Assets.Functionality: Internal single-bit start signal used to trigger the multiplier pipeline for FMUL processing and to seed its latency shift register.
Assets.Justification: multiplier.start controls the beginning of multi-cycle multiplication; if corrupted, the multiplier may operate on wrong operand states or at improper times causing incorrect product/results propagation to the normalizer. Ensuring the start signal's integrity prevents tampering with arithmetic execution.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit input carrying the second operand (integer-encoded single-precision float) used by arithmetic, min/max, compare and sign-inject units.
Assets.Justification: As with rs1_i, tampering with rs2_i changes arithmetic inputs and thus system results; integrity violations here lead to incorrect calculations and potentially wrong program behavior. Protecting rs2_i prevents data corruption attacks that alter computational outcomes.

Assets.Functionality: Two-bit comparator status from main ALU used by the FPU comparator logic to determine equal/less conditions for FEQ/FLT/FLE operations.
Assets.Justification: cmp_i encodes the ALU’s equality/ordering outcome consumed by the FPU; if altered or corrupted, FEQ/FLT/FLE would produce incorrect flags/results, misleading program decisions and violating computational correctness, so its integrity must be maintained.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit output delivering the final FPU operation result (classification, comparison, conversion or normalized/rounded arithmetic result) to the CPU pipeline.
Assets.Justification: If res_o is blocked, forced to constant values, or otherwise made unavailable at integration, the CPU cannot receive correct FP results and the operation effectively fails (denial-of-service for FP functionality). Ensuring availability of this output is required so the CPU can progress and consume computed data.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit handshake indicating that res_o contains a valid, completed operation result (asserted when ctrl_engine.valid is set).
Assets.Justification: If valid_o is blocked or not asserted, even correct res_o values will be ignored by the pipeline, effectively stalling or denying completion of FPU operations. Availability of the valid signal is therefore critical for the CPU to accept FPU results and maintain forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Internal aggregated done signal (OR of all FU done signals) used by the control engine to detect that the currently-started multi-cycle operation completed.
Assets.Justification: If fu_core_done is not asserted when operations finish (or is spuriously suppressed), the control FSM will not release the result (ctrl_engine.valid), preventing result delivery and causing a DoS of FPU operations. The availability of this completion indicator is essential for operation termination and handover to the CPU.

Assets.Functionality: Done handshake from the normalizer/rounder indicating that normalization, rounding or integer-to-float conversion has finished and result/flags are valid.
Assets.Justification: The normalizer is on the critical path for arithmetic and conversion results; if normalizer.done is prevented or held low the FPU cannot complete many operation classes and results never reach res_o/valid_o. Therefore maintaining availability of this done signal is necessary to avoid denial of FP services.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit operand source 1 provided from the register file; used as multiplicand or dividend and inspected for sign in signed operations.
Assets.Justification: Corruption/modification of rs1_i will directly change multiplication/division inputs and therefore produce incorrect results that propagate to the CPU state. The module relies on correct operand integrity to preserve correct arithmetic semantics.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit operand source 2 provided from the register file; used as multiplier or divisor and inspected for sign in signed operations.
Assets.Justification: If rs2_i is modified the multiplier/divider will compute wrong outputs (or divide by wrong/divisor), potentially producing incorrect program-visible state or triggering faults. Ensuring integrity of rs2_i is essential for correct arithmetic behavior.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit output presenting the computed result when the co-processor signals completion; contains lower/upper product bits for multiply or the division/remainder result depending on the operation and funct3 selection.
Assets.Justification: If the driven res_o is corrupted between the unit and the consuming stage (or the unit produces incorrect res_o), the register file or pipeline will receive wrong data. Preserving correctness of res_o is critical to maintain CPU state integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag indicating whether rs1 should be treated as signed for the current operation (affects sign compensation and initial abs conversion).
Assets.Justification: Incorrect signedness interpretation changes arithmetic semantics (e.g., abs conversion, sign compensation) and will produce wrong results. Maintaining correctness of this control bit is necessary for arithmetic integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag indicating whether rs2 should be treated as signed for the current operation (affects product/add/sub behavior and divisor absolute value).
Assets.Justification: If ctrl.rs2_is_signed is wrong, product or division algorithms perform incorrect sign handling (including negation/abs), leading to incorrect outputs. This directly impacts correctness of arithmetic results.

Assets.Functionality: Iteration/cycle counter stepping serial multiply/divide algorithms and detecting completion or abort conditions.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the cycle counter can cause premature termination or extra iterations of the serial algorithms, producing wrong results or corrupted intermediate state. The counter directly controls algorithm correctness.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the current remainder value in the iterative restoring division process; updated each cycle based on subtraction or restore operations.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the remainder register disrupts the intermediate division state and produces incorrect quotient or remainder results. Preserving its integrity is crucial for reliable arithmetic operations.

Assets.Functionality: Shift register for the working dividend/quotient during restoring division; progressively accumulates quotient bits over the iterations.
Assets.Justification: If this register is altered, the quotient bits accumulated during division become invalid, leading to an incorrect final result. Protecting its integrity ensures correct computation of division outcomes.

Assets.Functionality: Temporary wide vector that holds the trial subtraction result used to decide accept/restore operations within each division iteration.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with div.sub affects the compare/decision logic leading to incorrect accept/restore outcomes and thus incorrect quotient/remainder bits. Integrity protection prevents erroneous algorithmic decisions.

Assets.Functionality: 2*XLEN-bit product register used by parallel and iterative multiplier implementations to hold/accumulate the full multiplication result.
Assets.Justification: mul.prod holds the computed product; corruption here changes the final output halves selected for res_o. Integrity of this register is required to ensure correct multiplication results.

Assets.Functionality: Final division/remainder result after optional sign compensation, selected for delivery on res_o for div/rem operations.
Assets.Justification: div.res is the module's canonical division/rem result; corruption or incorrect sign compensation produces erroneous quotient/remainder values visible to the CPU. Its integrity is essential for correct divide/rem semantics.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle valid flag asserted when the unit finished the operation (S_DONE) to indicate res_o contains a valid result.
Assets.Justification: If valid_o is withheld or stuck low, the consumer will never accept results and the arithmetic operation is effectively denied, causing a denial-of-service of the M-extension operation. This flag gates the ability to commit results, so its availability is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Internal one-cycle enable produced by the FSM to permit driving final result onto res_o/valid_o (asserted in S_DONE).
Assets.Justification: ctrl.out_en directly gates when results are presented externally; preventing or forcing this signal can block outputs (DoS) or cause spurious outputs. As the integration-level point that enables final result delivery, its availability is dominant.

Assets.Functionality: FSM state (S_IDLE, S_BUSY, S_DONE) that sequences start, iterative processing, and one-cycle result output.
Assets.Justification: Forcing or blocking FSM transitions can prevent operations from starting or prevent the one-cycle output window, causing denial-of-service of multiply/divide operations. The FSM state is the primary sequencer for availability of results.

Assets.Functionality: Start signal asserted when a division/rem instruction is detected to initialize divider state and begin the iterative division sequence.
Assets.Justification: If div.start is prevented or spuriously asserted, divides/rem operations can be blocked or erroneously triggered, causing denial-of-service or spurious activity. As the entry point to the divider, its availability governs whether division can complete.

Assets.Functionality: Start signal asserted when a multiplication instruction is detected to initialize multiplier state and begin product computation.
Assets.Justification: Preventing mul.start blocks multiplication operations (DoS) while spurious starts may produce incorrect timing or outputs. This signal is the integration-level trigger for multiply operations, so its availability is critical.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit source operand fed into the serial shifter or the barrel shifter input layer; also provides the sign bit for arithmetic right shifts.
Assets.Justification: Altering rs1_i changes the data being shifted and therefore directly corrupts computation results; an integrator would consider the correctness of this operand critical. Because rs1_i is an input that controls the value transformed by the shifter, its integrity is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Supplies the shift distance controlling how many bit positions the operand is shifted (loaded into the serial counter or used to select barrel-shifter mux layers).
Assets.Justification: Corrupting shamt_i directly changes the executed shift operation (magnitude of shift) and therefore can silently change computational results or break software assumptions. As a control input that modifies data transformation, ensuring its integrity is essential.

Assets.Functionality: Presents the final shifted value produced by the module to the rest of the CPU (driven either from the serial shifter when done or from the barrel-shifter result).
Assets.Justification: If res_o is blocked or not produced when expected, downstream units cannot obtain required computation results and processor execution would be disrupted (denial-of-service impact). Although output integrity matters, the dominant integration-level concern is that the result must be available when expected for correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates when res_o contains a valid completed shift result (derived from done/done_ff for serial and from valid_cmd for barrel implementation).
Assets.Justification: valid_o is used by the CPU to determine when it can consume res_o; if this signal is unavailable or stuck inactive, the processor cannot progress or will wait indefinitely, causing a denial-of-service. Thus availability of this handshake/status signal is critical at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the operand and intermediate shift state in the serial-shifter implementation; loaded from rs1_i at start and updated each cycle until the operation completes.
Assets.Justification: sreg stores the live intermediate computation result; any corruption while an operation is in-flight will alter the final output and break correctness. Protecting the integrity of this internal register is necessary because it directly determines the produced result.

Assets.Functionality: Counts remaining shift steps for the serial shifter (loaded from shamt_i on start and decremented each shift cycle) and governs run/done behaviour.
Assets.Justification: If shifter.cnt is tampered with, the number of performed shifts changes, causing incorrect results or premature/late completion; thus its correctness is integral to correct operation. The counter directly controls the data transformation sequence, making integrity the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Registered combination of busy and done used to generate a one-cycle-stable result-valid condition and to gate the serial output (res_o) when a serial operation completes.
Assets.Justification: done_ff controls when the completed serial result is presented; if it is stuck or suppressed the valid one-cycle result and res_o will be withheld, preventing consumption of the result and causing functional stall. Therefore availability (timely presentation of results) is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Arbitration/state flag indicating that a serial shift operation is in progress (prevents new triggers and is used to derive done_ff/valid_o); also used to abort on trap.
Assets.Justification: shifter.busy gates new requests and qualifies done/valid generation; if stuck high or low, the unit either never accepts/completes shifts or accepts overlapping triggers that break sequencing, causing stalls, livelock, or dropped operations—directly impacting forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Clocked register that captures the final barrel-shifter stage output (before optional bit-reverse) and supplies the module's res_o in the barrel implementation.
Assets.Justification: bs_result holds the registered final shift result for the fast-path; unauthorized corruption of this register will produce incorrect outputs consumed by the CPU. Protecting the integrity of this register is essential because it directly determines the output value in the barrel-shifter mode.

Assets.Functionality: Array of XLEN-bit vectors that implement the stage-wise muxing and data propagation for the barrel (fast) shifter; they form the intermediate data that is combined according to shamt_i bits to produce the final shifted value.
Assets.Justification: bs_level holds the intermediate transformation of input bits in the barrel path; corrupting these values changes the final computed output and therefore breaks correctness. Integrity of these internal data paths is the main concern.

Assets.Functionality: 16-bit compressed instruction input that the decompressor reads and decodes to assemble the 32-bit instruction and immediates.
Assets.Justification: An attacker or faulty integrator that can modify instr_i will directly change the decoded 32-bit instruction and thus the processor's executed behavior. Maintaining integrity of this input is required to prevent instruction corruption, unintended control-flow changes, or arbitrary code execution.

Assets.Functionality: Internal 32-bit signal that holds the assembled/pre-decoded instruction built from instr_i and immediates; this value is propagated to instr_o (subject to 'illegal').
Assets.Justification: Corruption or unauthorized modification of 'decoded' will change what is presented on instr_o and thus what the processor executes. Ensuring integrity of this internal state is necessary to prevent execution of altered or malicious instructions.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag set during decompression checks to indicate the compressed instruction is illegal; when asserted it forces instr_o[1] to '0' to reflect an illegal encoding.
Assets.Justification: If 'illegal' is tampered with, illegal encodings could be hidden or valid encodings could be falsely reported, altering instruction semantics delivered to the CPU. Integrity of this flag is required to ensure correctness of illegal-instruction detection and the resulting output encoding.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit decompressed instruction output driven from the internal decoded word (bits[31:2] mirror decoded; bit[1] is forced to '0' when an illegal compressed instruction is detected).
Assets.Justification: If instr_o is blocked, held, or otherwise made unavailable to the downstream execution unit, the CPU will not receive valid instructions and normal operation can be denied. Availability of this output is therefore critical to prevent denial-of-service at the instruction delivery boundary.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the current word-aligned program counter used to generate ibus_req_o.addr and incremented on successful fetch responses to point to the next instruction word.
Assets.Justification: Corrupting the PC would cause the frontend to fetch incorrect instruction words, directly changing program flow and breaking execution correctness. Because it controls which instructions are fetched, its integrity is critical to system correctness and security.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered restart flag set on reset or branch (ctrl_i.if_reset) that clears/initializes IPB and forces the fetch and issue engines to reinitialize to a new PC.
Assets.Justification: Forcing repeated or persistent restarts prevents forward progress by clearing the prefetch buffer and reinitializing the fetch pipeline, effectively causing a denial-of-service of instruction delivery. Thus manipulation of this flag primarily impacts availability of normal operation.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered privilege level used for outstanding instruction bus accesses (propagated to ibus_req_o.priv) and set on restarts from ctrl_i.cpu_priv.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the privileged level used for fetches could cause instruction fetches with incorrect privileges (e.g., escalate or de-escalate fetch privilege), potentially causing incorrect memory access semantics or exposing privileged code paths. Maintaining the integrity of this field is therefore required to ensure correct privilege-separated behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Local flag indicating receipt of a bus response (ack or err); used by the fetch FSM to advance the PC and trigger writes into the prefetch buffer.
Assets.Justification: If fetch.resp is corrupted, the frontend may wrongly advance the PC or write invalid data into the IPB, leading to incorrect instruction sequences being delivered to the backend. Thus the correctness of fetch sequencing depends on this signal's integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Per-entry free signals from the FIFO indicating available space; used by the fetch FSM to determine whether to issue new bus requests and to set frontend halted when insufficient space exists.
Assets.Justification: Falsely indicating the FIFO is full (or otherwise manipulating free signals) prevents further fetch requests and can halt instruction intake, causing the frontend/back-end to stall. Hence these status signals primarily affect availability of instruction flow.

Assets.Functionality: Per-entry availability flags that indicate valid half-word data present in the FIFO; used by the issue engine to assert frontend_o.valid and decide when to assemble/issue instructions.
Assets.Justification: Suppressing availability (making entries appear empty) prevents the issue engine from presenting instructions to the backend even though data exists, stalling instruction issuance. Thus these indicators are crucial to maintaining availability of instruction delivery.

Assets.Functionality: Input control signal that, when asserted together with the ICC data CSR address, triggers writes of csr_wdata_i into the outgoing TX FIFO (drives tx_fifo_we).
Assets.Justification: csr_we_i directly enables modification of the TX FIFO contents by causing writes of software-provided data into the outgoing message queue. If corrupted or asserted incorrectly, it can introduce or alter messages transmitted between cores, thereby compromising the integrity of inter-core data.

Assets.Asset Name: CSR Read Enable (TX link acknowledge control)
Assets.Functionality: Input control signal used to acknowledge TX link reads: it causes icc_tx_o.ack to be asserted when the ICC data CSR is read and drives FIFO read behavior (fifo read enable).
Assets.Justification: csr_re_i gates read/transfer operations from the TX FIFO; if it is unavailable or blocked, outgoing transfers cannot be acknowledged/read and the TX path can be effectively disabled, producing a denial-of-service for inter-core message transmission. Malicious or missing assertions therefore primarily impact the module's availability to send data.

Assets.Functionality: Internal control signal asserted when a CSR write to the ICC data register occurs (derived from csr_we_i & address match); it enables pushing csr_wdata_i into the tx_queue_inst FIFO.
Assets.Justification: tx_fifo_we is the immediate control that inserts data into the outgoing FIFO; tampering or unintended assertion can corrupt the FIFO contents or cause unintended messages to be enqueued, directly affecting the integrity of data exchanged between cores.

Assets.Functionality: Status signal from the outgoing TX FIFO (free_o) that indicates available free space and is sampled into the ICC control/status CSR so software can determine if the FIFO accepts more data.
Assets.Justification: tx_fifo_free is used by software to decide whether it can write more data; if this indicator is missing, suppressed, or forged, software may be prevented from sending messages or may overflow the FIFO, resulting in denial-of-service or disrupted inter-core communication, making availability the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Input address captured into the Memory Address Register (MAR) on lsu_mo_we; used for alignment checks, byte-enable calculation and supplied as the bus address for load/store transactions.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or malicious modification of addr_i will cause the LSU to target incorrect memory addresses, producing incorrect reads/writes and possible memory corruption. Because addr_i directly determines which memory locations are accessed, its integrity is critical to correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: Provides write-data used to form the bus request payload (data field) with alignment/replication for sub-word stores and is used as the operand for atomic memory operations.
Assets.Justification: If wdata_i is altered, the data written to memory will be corrupted or incorrect, directly compromising the integrity of stored state. Since wdata_i is the source of store payloads and AMO operands, its correct value is required to maintain memory integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Internal register that latches the access address (from addr_i) and is used as the bus address, for alignment checks, and to select the correct byte/half-word when forming read data.
Assets.Justification: MAR holds the canonical address for the current memory access; corruption of MAR will result in wrong addresses being issued on the bus and incorrect data being read or written. Because it is the latched source of address decisions, its integrity is essential for correct LSU behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Encoded AMO opcode derived from ir_funct12 that is forwarded to the bus request (dbus_req_o.amoop) to specify the semantic of atomic memory operations (LR/SC/ADD/AND/OR/MIN/MAX/etc.).
Assets.Justification: If amo_cmd is altered, the semantic of performed AMOs changes (for example ADD -> AND), leading to incorrect memory updates and corrupted shared state. Because AMOs change read-modify-write behavior atomically, the correctness of their encoding is a critical integrity property.

Assets.Functionality: Physical Memory Protection fault input that is OR'ed into arbiter_err and prevents issuing the bus strobe (dbus_req_o.stb) when asserted.
Assets.Justification: When pmp_fault_i is asserted it inhibits bus strobe generation and contributes to arbiter errors, effectively blocking memory accesses; a persistent or malicious assertion therefore denies service to the CPU. Thus pmp_fault_i is an integration-level attack point that can be used to create a DoS on the LSU.

Assets.Functionality: Handshaking signal asserted while the LSU is waiting for the bus response (driven as not dbus_rsp_i.ack) to indicate the CPU must stall until the access completes.
Assets.Justification: If wait_o is held asserted (or mis-driven) the CPU will be stalled and forward progress will be prevented, producing a denial-of-service at the processor level. Because wait_o directly controls CPU stalling behavior, it is availability-critical to system operation.

Assets.Functionality: Flag set when the latched address (MAR) is misaligned for the requested access size; used to inhibit bus strobe (preventing the access) and to report misaligned load/store errors.
Assets.Justification: If misaligned is spuriously asserted, the LSU will withhold issuing bus transactions (dbus_req_o.stb is gated by not misaligned), causing legitimate accesses to be blocked and resulting in a DoS. Therefore, the correctness/availability of this signal is required for normal operation.

Assets.Functionality: Latches a pending LSU bus request (set from ctrl_i.lsu_req and cleared on bus acknowledge or trap); it gates read-data capture and is used to generate wait and error conditions.
Assets.Justification: If arbiter_req is stuck asserted or stuck deasserted, the LSU will either never accept new requests or never clear outstanding requests, both of which prevent normal operation and create a denial-of-service. Because it controls whether the LSU is considered busy, its correct behavior is critical to availability.

Assets.Functionality: Reports four access/alignment and bus/PMP error conditions (misaligned load/store and load/store bus errors) to the control unit while an access is pending.
Assets.Justification: err_o communicates alignment, bus, and PMP faults to the control unit; if tampered (suppressed, spurious, or bit-flipped), the CPU may either commit an illegal access or trap unnecessarily, breaking architectural guarantees and enabling silent corruption or bypass of memory-protection checks.

Assets.Functionality: Delivers aligned and sign/zero-extended data from the data-bus response to the CPU after selecting bytes/half-words/words based on MAR and funct3.
Assets.Justification: rdata_o is the value the core consumes after byte-lane selection and sign/zero extension; any corruption or mis-selection yields incorrect load results, causing silent state corruption and incorrect program behavior, so its integrity must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered error flag combining dbus_rsp_i.err and pmp_fault_i that contributes to error reporting and influences request lifecycle.
Assets.Justification: arbiter_err feeds into err_o and represents bus/PMP error status; masking or falsifying this internal error state will lead to incorrect error reporting and handling, allowing failed accesses to appear successful or vice versa, compromising correctness of error semantics (integrity).

Assets.Functionality: Array of 8-bit per-region configuration registers that store R/W/X permission bits, mode bits (OFF/TOR/NA4/NAPOT), reserved bits and the lock (L) bit. These registers determine how each PMP region behaves and whether entries are writable or locked.
Assets.Justification: pmpcfg holds the authoritative permission and mode settings for all PMP regions; unauthorized modification of these bits (R/W/X/A/L) directly changes access control decisions and can either disable protection or incorrectly allow accesses. Protecting the integrity of pmpcfg is therefore essential to preserve the PMP security policy.

Assets.Functionality: Array of XLEN-bit per-region address registers (PMPADDR) that define region boundaries/masks used for TOR / NA4 / NAPOT matching. These values are used by the matching logic to determine whether a given access falls into a protected region.
Assets.Justification: pmpaddr values define memory region boundaries; corrupting or overwriting these registers can expand, shrink or move protected regions and thereby allow unauthorized memory accesses or deny expected accesses. Maintaining their integrity is necessary to ensure the PMP enforces the intended memory protection policy.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit input that supplies the address of the current load/store operation to be checked by the PMP (selected into acc_addr when checking data accesses). It is compared against configured PMP regions for permission evaluation.
Assets.Justification: The correctness of the address used for permission checking is critical: if addr_ls_i is tampered with or provided incorrectly, region matching may be bypassed or misapplied causing either unauthorized memory accesses or spurious faults. Thus the address input must be protected from corruption to ensure accurate permission enforcement.

Assets.Functionality: Internal signal that selects the privilege level used for the current access (either fetch privilege or LSU-provided privilege) and is used by permission logic to apply M-mode exceptions or normal permission checks.
Assets.Justification: acc_priv changes how allow(r) is computed (M-mode may bypass locked entries); if this signal were corrupted to indicate a higher privilege, accesses could be improperly permitted, undermining PMP protections. Therefore integrity of acc_priv is required to ensure correct permission decisions.

Assets.Functionality: Synchronous output flag that signals a permission violation (PMP fault) for the currently checked access, with debug-mode suppression. This output is used by the CPU to react to PMP violations (e.g., raise exceptions or block access).
Assets.Justification: fault_o directly affects whether the CPU perceives and acts upon PMP violations: a stuck-asserted or spuriously asserted fault can deny legitimate operation (DoS), while a permanently suppressed fault can hide violations. The dominant risk is availability impact because incorrect fault signaling can block or disrupt normal CPU memory operations.

Assets.Functionality: Priority chain vector that aggregates per-region deny decisions (starting from lowest priority) and computes the final failure result used to drive fault_o; implements static prioritization of PMP regions.
Assets.Justification: The fail chain is the structural logic that decides whether an access triggers a PMP fault; corruption or manipulation of this chain can cause spurious faults (blocking execution) or suppress real faults. Its correct operation is therefore critical to avoid denial-of-service or loss of expected fault signaling, making availability the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit destination data input that is written into a selected register file entry when write enable is asserted.
Assets.Justification: rd_i provides the data that updates register file entries. If rd_i is corrupted or manipulated, register contents will be modified incorrectly, directly corrupting CPU state and program behavior, so integrity is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Array of general-purpose registers (32 entries for RV32I or 16 for RV32E) that stores operands, intermediate results and program-visible state.
Assets.Justification: reg_file holds the authoritative CPU state (general-purpose registers). Any corruption or unauthorized modification of these memory cells changes program-visible state and computation results, so integrity protection is the primary requirement.

Assets.Functionality: Internal single-bit write enable signal that gates writes into reg_file (derived from control signals and x0 protection logic).
Assets.Justification: rf_we determines whether rd_i is written into reg_file. Faults or manipulation that force or suppress rf_we can cause unintended writes or prevent legitimate updates, corrupting register state; thus integrity is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Multiplexed address (rs1 or rd or forced-zero) used to index the register file for the synchronous read and for write destination selection in the FPGA-style variant.
Assets.Justification: opa_addr selects which register is read or written via the shared port; tampering or misselection can cause writes to or reads from wrong registers, corrupting CPU state and operation. Therefore integrity is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag indicating that the current destination address is x0; used to prevent normal writes to the zero register unless explicitly forced.
Assets.Justification: rd_zero prevents accidental modification of the architectural x0 register. If this signal is compromised (e.g., suppressed or stuck), writes to x0 might occur or prevented when intended, altering architectural guarantees and corrupting state, so integrity is the primary risk.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit synchronous source operand output delivering the register value selected by rf_rs1 to the rest of the CPU datapath.
Assets.Justification: rs1_o is required by downstream execution units to obtain operands; if this port is blocked, tied-off or withheld at integration, instructions cannot execute correctly, causing denial-of-service or halted CPU progress. Availability is the dominant risk for this observable port.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit synchronous source operand output delivering the register value selected by rf_rs2 to the rest of the CPU datapath.
Assets.Justification: Like rs1_o, rs2_o is required for instruction execution; if rs2_o is made unavailable or corrupted at integration level, many instructions will fail to execute, producing a denial-of-service. Hence availability is the dominant concern.
