Assets.Functionality: Internal signal derived from ctrl_i.ir_funct12(11 downto 7) that selects which register is read for the optional rs3_o port.
Assets.Justification: rs3_addr determines which register value is presented on rs3_o. If this address is manipulated, instructions will read incorrect operands leading to incorrect computation and corrupted state, so integrity is the main concern.

Assets.Functionality: Input write-enable signal that, when high on a clock edge (and when enable_i is high), allows wdata_i(0) to be sampled and used to set the internal authenticated state.
Assets.Justification: we_i directly controls whether an external write can modify the authenticator's state (authenticated_q). If an attacker can toggle/weirdly drive this signal they can cause unauthorized changes to authentication state (e.g., inject a write that sets authenticated_q), so it must be protected as an integrity-critical control.

Assets.Functionality: Input enable signal for the authenticator; when low it immediately clears the authenticated state and disables updates, and when high normal authentication updates are permitted.
Assets.Justification: enable_i can be used at integration level to clear authentication or prevent authenticating writes, effectively denying access to the on-chip debugger. Because forcing or withholding this signal can produce a denial-of-service on debug access, its dominant concern is availability.

Assets.Functionality: Output that reflects the authenticated state (driven from authenticated_q); when high it indicates authentication passed and unlocks the on-chip debugger.
Assets.Justification: valid_o is the observable/unlocking signal used by the debug module; if it is unavailable, stuck low, or suppressed at integration, the debugger remains locked and normal debug functionality is denied, making this port availability-critical.

Assets.Functionality: Internal single-bit register that stores whether authentication has passed; it is set from wdata_i(0) when we_i and enable_i allow, and cleared by reset or when enable_i is low.
Assets.Justification: authenticated_q is the authoritative state that gates debug access; unauthorized modification of this internal signal (or its incorrect update) directly compromises the correctness of authentication, so its integrity must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: Output indicating the authenticator is busy; in this implementation it is permanently driven low, but conceptually it can block further read/write accesses while high.
Assets.Justification: busy_o governs whether new transactions may proceed; if asserted or stuck high, legitimate accesses are blocked and the system can stall, while if suppressed when the unit is actually busy, overlapping operations can cause retries or lockups—both directly harming forward progress and availability (even if this instance ties the signal low).

Assets.Functionality: Per-hart vector output that requests each hart to halt and enter debug mode; it is gated by hart selection, DM active state and authentication when enabled.
Assets.Justification: Assertion of halt_req_o can stop execution of the targeted hart(s), thereby denying normal operation (DoS). Because the debugger interface drives this signal, an attacker who can influence the related control path can disrupt system availability by repeatedly halting harts.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit data buffer used as the abstract data0 exchange between the debugger and the hart; it can be written by the DM (DMI) or by the CPU bus and read via DMI/bus.
Assets.Justification: This register is used as the intermediary for GPR <-> DM transfers and for abstract write operations that can modify hart registers/memory; corruption or unauthorized modification of dci.data_reg can directly alter CPU state and program behavior, compromising integrity of the system state.

Assets.Functionality: Contains the abstract command written via DMI that instructs the DM to perform register/memory transfers (fields include cmdtype, transfer, write, regno, aarsize, postexec). It drives the DM command execution FSM.
Assets.Justification: dm_reg.command controls which registers/memory locations are accessed and whether data is read or written. If modified or injected with incorrect values it can cause unintended reads/writes or privilege-violating operations, so the primary concern is integrity of this control word.

Assets.Asset Name: NDM System Reset Control (SoC reset output)
Assets.Functionality: Active-low SoC reset output driven by the DM ndmreset control (when DM is active and authentication permits) to assert a system-level reset of the SoC.
Assets.Justification: ndmrstn_o drives a chip-wide reset; if forced low spuriously it can continuously reset the SoC and deny service, while if it cannot be asserted when needed (despite dmactive and valid auth) the system cannot recover from faulted states, both directly compromising availability.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates successful authentication when the optional authenticator is enabled; it gates authenticated DMI register read/write access (dmi_*_auth signals).
Assets.Justification: auth.valid controls whether privileged DMI accesses are allowed; if an attacker can set or spoof auth.valid, they obtain write/read capabilities to critical DM registers (progbuf, command, data0), enabling unauthorized modifications and thus breaching system integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Drives the serial output bit on TCK falling edges to present the LSB of the selected instruction/data register (idcode, dtmcs, dmi or bypass) to the JTAG host.
Assets.Justification: TDO is the primary debug output path; if TDO is blocked, driven incorrectly, or withheld, external debuggers cannot observe register or device state, preventing normal debug/read-back workflows and effectively denying service.

Assets.Functionality: Contains DTM control bits (e.g., dmihardreset, dmireset) and status fields; it is written via the DR and used to control/reset the DMI interface and report status back to the host.
Assets.Justification: DTMCS governs resets and status of the debug transport; if its contents are corrupted or spoofed, the DMI can be reset spuriously or status misreported, desynchronizing host–target control and causing unintended state transitions—hence its integrity must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: 7-bit address used by the DTM to specify the target register inside the debug module for read/write DMI transactions.
Assets.Justification: The address determines where read/write operations land inside the debug module; corruption or manipulation of this field can cause writes/reads to unintended registers, leading to corrupted configuration or unauthorized access to internal state.

Assets.Functionality: When shifted/written it contains the DMI operation, address and write data which are sampled and forwarded to the dmi_controller to initiate DMI read/write transactions.
Assets.Justification: tap_reg.dmi holds the target address, payload and command for DMI operations; any tampering while shifting or capturing these bits can redirect or corrupt DMI transactions, modifying which debug-module register is accessed and what data/command is executed.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates that a DMI transaction is in progress and prevents new DMI accesses until the current operation completes; used to arbitrate and stall additional requests.
Assets.Justification: If the busy flag is stuck or incorrectly asserted, new DMI operations are prevented (the controller treats the interface as occupied), effectively causing a denial-of-service on DMI accesses and blocking debug interactions.

Assets.Functionality: Selects TAP state transitions (driving the TAP state machine); it is synchronized and used on TCK edges to move between JTAG states (e.g., SHIFT, UPDATE, RUN_IDLE).
Assets.Justification: TMS determines TAP state progression; malicious or erroneous control of TMS can prevent entering required states (e.g., DR_UPDATE) or lock the TAP, effectively denying debugging operations and blocking access to the debug interface.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit operation code that encodes the requested DMI action (e.g., NOP, read, write) forwarded to the debug module.
Assets.Justification: The op field determines whether a DMI access is a read or write (or noop); tampering with op can convert harmless accesses into destructive writes or prevent expected reads, compromising control-flow and data correctness of debug transactions.

Assets.Functionality: Four byte-wide memory arrays that store the DMEM contents (bits 7..0, 15..8, 23..16, 31..24). They are written selectively using bus_req_i.ben and provide the four bytes assembled into the 32-bit read word.
Assets.Justification: These arrays are the authoritative storage for DMEM; any unintended write-enable decoding (bus_req_i.ben) or index corruption will modify the stored bytes and propagate incorrect words to rdata, causing silent memory corruption.

Assets.Functionality: Combinatorially derived unsigned word-aligned index taken from bus_req_i.addr(addr_hi_c downto 2) used to index the byte memories for reads (default style) and writes.
Assets.Justification: addr selects which word is read or written; if altered or miscomputed, accesses target the wrong location so writes corrupt unintended words and reads return incorrect data, violating memory correctness.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit vector that collects the four byte-wide memory outputs (mem_ram_b0..b3 or via addr_ff) and supplies the read data that is presented on the bus response.
Assets.Justification: rdata forms the word returned to the CPU; any corruption, byte-lane swap, or misalignment during assembly yields an incorrect value on the bus response, resulting in silent state corruption.

Assets.Functionality: Clocked flag that is asserted when a bus request is valid and indicates a read; used to gate bus_rsp_o.data timing (bus_rsp_o.data <= rdata when rden = '1').
Assets.Justification: rden gates when read data is driven; if stuck low or suppressed, reads never complete and the core stalls, while spurious assertion can produce retries/lockups—both directly degrading forward progress and availability.

Assets.Functionality: Four byte-wide RAM slices that together implement the 32-bit instruction memory when IMEM is configured as RAM. Each slice stores one byte of the instruction word. Writes are selective via bus_req_i.ben, and reads assemble the four slices into rdata.
Assets.Justification: These slices are the authoritative program store; any unintended write-enable, bit flip, or byte-lane corruption alters opcodes/immediates and can redirect control flow or execute unintended code, so code-store integrity is critical.

Assets.Functionality: A 32-bit register that captures and outputs instruction words from IMEM (ROM or RAM). It updates on clock edges and is driven on bus responses when reads are active.
Assets.Justification: rdata is the instruction presented to fetch/decode; corruption, stale sampling, or byte-lane mix-ups yield the wrong opcode to the CPU, causing incorrect execution, so its integrity must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: Word-aligned address derived from bus_req_i.addr(addr_hi_c downto 2). Used to index instruction memory for both reads and writes.
Assets.Justification: addr selects which instruction word is fetched or written; if manipulated or computed incorrectly, the core fetches from the wrong location, enabling code redirection or silent corruption.

Assets.Functionality: A single-bit registered signal derived from bus_req_i.stb and not bus_req_i.rw. It gates whether rdata is driven onto bus_rsp_o.data.
Assets.Justification: rden governs when instruction data is driven; if stuck low, instruction fetches never complete and the pipeline stalls, while spurious assertion can cause fetch glitches—both degrading forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Full 32-bit access address used by the cache memory to extract tag, index and word offset for tag/status lookup and data memory addressing.
Assets.Justification: addr_i determines the tag, set index, and word offset; if corrupted, the cache targets the wrong line/word, returning stale data or overwriting unrelated entries, thereby violating data correctness.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit byte-wide write-enable vector that controls which bytes of the currently addressed 32-bit word are written into the byte-sliced data sub-memories.
Assets.Justification: we_i selects which byte lanes are updated; any bit flip can drop intended updates or clobber adjacent bytes, causing silent corruption in the cache (and later in memory on write-back).

Assets.Functionality: Command input to invalidate the currently addressed cache block (clears its valid flag) for flush/error operations.
Assets.Justification: inval_i controls the valid flag of a line; spurious invalidation discards correct data and forces misses, while suppression leaves stale/poisoned lines marked valid, both leading to incorrect read results.

Assets.Functionality: Command input to mark the currently addressed block as dirty (set dirty flag), used on cache write hits (disabled when READ_ONLY = true).
Assets.Justification: dirty_i records whether a line holds modified data; if cleared when updates occurred, evictions can lose writes (no write-back), and if asserted spuriously, clean lines may be written back or mis-handled, both corrupting architectural state.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered request flag that latches an incoming host request across FSM cycles so the controller can service pending accesses.
Assets.Justification: ctrl.buf_req preserves a pending access across controller cycles; if it fails to capture or to clear, requests are dropped or never retire, causing stalls, starvation, or replay loops that impede forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered fence/sync flag used to remember a pending cache flush/synchronization request across FSM transitions.
Assets.Justification: ctrl.buf_sync ensures fence/flush commands complete; if lost, ordered operations cannot proceed and the system can hang waiting for completion, while if stuck asserted the controller may repeatedly flush and block normal traffic—both degrading availability.

Assets.Functionality: Status input from the cache memory indicating whether the current access address results in a cache hit; used by the controller to decide read/write behavior and whether to initiate replacement or direct responses.
Assets.Justification: sta_hit steers the controller between immediate service and miss/refill paths; if suppressed or incorrect, the FSM can wait for nonexistent data or thrash into needless refills, causing long stalls and loss of throughput.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level output that signals the cache is fully synchronized with memory and contains no dirty lines; asserted by the controller when the internal cache reports clean status and the control engine is idle.
Assets.Justification: As the completion signal for cache flush and synchronization, clean_o must remain reliable. If stuck low, fence instructions may stall indefinitely, causing denial of service. If raised prematurely while dirty lines remain, the system resumes too early, leading to repeated retries or fault conditions. Its correctness is essential to guarantee forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Controls which host port (A when '0', B when '1') is connected to the downstream device; used by request/response switching and gating ACK/ERR back to the correct host.
Assets.Justification: If 'sel' is corrupted an access from one master can be routed to the other master or responses (ACK/ERR) can be mis-gated, changing which core receives data and status. This directly modifies the control/data flow and can cause incorrect behavior or data corruption, so integrity is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Strobe asserted to the downstream device (x_req_o.stb) when the arbiter grants a host port access; initiates the forwarded transaction.
Assets.Justification: If 'stb' is suppressed or spuriously asserted the downstream transaction can be blocked or injected, resulting in denial-of-service or unintended operations. The primary impact is preventing or enabling progress of accesses, making availability the dominant objective.

Assets.Functionality: Latched request indicator for host port A that stores incoming A strobes until the arbiter services them or clears them when A is granted.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with 'a_req' can cause A's requests to be lost or permanently stalled (DoS) or create spurious requests that flood the bus; the main consequence is preventing legitimate A accesses, so availability is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Latched request indicator for host port B that stores incoming B strobes until the arbiter services them or clears them when B is granted.
Assets.Justification: Analogous to a_req, corruption of 'b_req' can block or fabricate requests for port B and thereby deny service or create bus contention; availability impact is most significant.

Assets.Functionality: Signal indicating whether the current core request is a reservation-set operation (LR/SC variant) derived from the request's AMO encoding.
Assets.Justification: rvso gates special LR/SC handling and decides if SC stores are permitted; if rvso is wrong, LR/SC sequences may be misinterpreted and atomic synchronization semantics will be violated, leading to data corruption in concurrent code.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit vector that indicates which section (A,B,C or X) the incoming host request address maps to; used to steer the request to the matching section port.
Assets.Justification: If 'port_sel' is manipulated an access can be routed to the wrong section or to the void X port, causing accesses to reach incorrect peripherals or bypass intended targets; this corrupts address-to-device mapping and thus primarily threatens integrity of memory/IO routing.

Assets.Functionality: Local error flag set by the keeper when a timeout or device error is detected; exposed as the host response error (rsp_o.err) to signal bus errors to the CPU.
Assets.Justification: False positives in 'keeper.err' will report spurious bus errors and can cause the CPU to abort or retry transactions unnecessarily, effectively denying correct service; conversely clearing real errors can hide failures. The dominant impact is on availability of correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: Indicator used to disable timeout counting for accesses directed to the X (void) port; when asserted the keeper will not time out the access.
Assets.Justification: If 'keeper.halt' is forced erroneously, real timeouts may be suppressed allowing hung accesses to remain undetected and blocking progress; if cleared wrongly, legitimate long-running accesses may be timed out — both cause availability issues, making availability dominant.

Assets.Functionality: Computed result of the AMO read-modify-write ALU that is written back to memory during the write phase of an AMO operation.
Assets.Justification: If 'alu_res' is manipulated the value written back for AMO operations will be incorrect, leading to corrupted memory state and violated atomic operation semantics; this is a clear integrity threat.

Assets.Functionality: Internal register that stores the write operand (host-provided data) for the AMO sequence; used together with the pre-read rdata to compute the final write value.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with 'arbiter.wdata' changes the computed AMO result and the value written back during the atomic write phase, corrupting memory contents and breaking atomic semantics; integrity is the dominant impact.

Assets.Functionality: Tracks whether a global LR reservation is active and handles LR/SC transitions and invalidation for the reservation-set controller.
Assets.Justification: Corrupting the reservation FSM 'state' can incorrectly allow or disallow store-conditional (SC) commits or invalidate reservations improperly, breaking atomicity guarantees for LR/SC sequences and thus compromising operation integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Drives the 32-bit target address on the external Wishbone-compatible bus derived from the internal transaction address (bus_req.addr).
Assets.Justification: xbus_adr_o selects the external target; any corruption misaddresses requests, causing reads from or writes to unintended devices/locations and silently corrupting system state.

Assets.Functionality: Outputs 32-bit write data to the external bus for store/write transactions (driven from bus_req.data).
Assets.Justification: xbus_dat_o carries the value committed to peripherals/memory; if altered, the system stores incorrect data, breaking end-to-end correctness guarantees.

Assets.Functionality: Receives 32-bit read data from the external device and is forwarded into the internal bus response (bus_rsp.data) when a transaction is pending.
Assets.Justification: xbus_dat_i becomes the CPU-visible read value; spoofing or corruption injects wrong data into architectural state, leading to silent malfunction.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit signal indicating direction of transfer (read=0 / write=1) for external transactions, driven from bus_req.rw.
Assets.Justification: xbus_we_o encodes operation direction; a flip turns reads into unintended writes (or vice versa), causing data loss or missed updates.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit byte-enable mask signaling which bytes of the 32-bit word are active for the transfer (driven from bus_req.ben).
Assets.Justification: xbus_sel_o chooses active byte lanes; errors drop intended bytes or overwrite adjacent lanes, producing partial-word corruption.

Assets.Functionality: Strobe asserting a valid single transfer request on the external bus (driven from bus_req.stb); part of the pipelined Wishbone interface.
Assets.Justification: xbus_stb_o launches transfers; if suppressed the bus never issues requests (stall), while if stuck high it can monopolize the bus or create protocol violations, degrading throughput.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates a valid bus cycle and is asserted while a transfer is active (driven as bus_req.stb OR pending(1)) to hold cycles across multi-step/atomic accesses.
Assets.Justification: xbus_cyc_o holds the bus during active/atomic sequences; incorrect assertion/deassertion can hang the bus or prematurely end cycles, stalling forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Acknowledge from the external device indicating transfer completion; used to generate bus_rsp.ack and to advance/complete pending transactions and atomic sequences.
Assets.Justification: xbus_ack_i completes handshakes; if missing, requests never retire (stall), while spurious acks can advance state without valid data, leading to retries or lockups.

Assets.Functionality: Error indication from the external device used to set bus_rsp.err and to abort/clear pending transactions and timeouts.
Assets.Justification: xbus_err_i terminates faulty transactions; if suppressed, the controller may wait indefinitely, and if asserted spuriously, valid traffic is aborted—both harming availability.

Assets.Functionality: Internal two-bit vector tracking pending/atomic transaction state used to gate responses (bus_rsp) and to compute xbus_cyc_o behavior.
Assets.Justification: pending tracks in-flight/atomic sequences; corruption can keep the bus busy forever or drop cycles early, causing deadlock or lost operations.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag asserted when the timeout counter reaches TIMEOUT_VAL to signal an unacknowledged access and produce a bus error/abort.
Assets.Justification: timeout bounds wait time; if never asserted, the bus can hang on unresponsive devices, and if asserted prematurely, valid transactions are aborted—both reducing availability.

Assets.Functionality: Internal cycle counter that is incremented while a transaction is pending and compared against TIMEOUT_VAL to generate the timeout flag.
Assets.Justification: timecnt drives timeout detection; incorrect counting delays or prevents aborts (hang) or triggers early timeouts (spurious aborts), impairing forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Vector output that drives the external GPIO pins with the values coming from the module's output register (port_out). It is the physical interface used by external devices to observe/control state driven by the SoC.
Assets.Justification: If gpio_o is blocked, held inactive, or otherwise made unavailable at integration, external devices will not receive the expected control signals and the GPIO’s role in the system is effectively denied. The primary impact is loss of outward functionality (denial-of-service), so availability is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Vector input sampled into the module (into port_in) and used for bus read-back and interrupt generation. It represents external events and sensor/status signals sampled by the processor.
Assets.Justification: If gpio_i is manipulated (spoofed or corrupted), the sampled values and resulting IRQ decisions can be wrong, causing false or missing event detection. The main concern is unauthorized modification of input data that changes system behavior, so integrity is dominant.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit output that is asserted when any enabled GPIO pending interrupt bit is set (irq_pend reduction), serving as the module’s interrupt to the CPU.
Assets.Justification: If cpu_irq_o is suppressed or disabled at integration, the CPU will not be notified of GPIO events and the interrupt-driven functionality is denied. This is primarily a denial-of-service effect on the CPU notification channel, so availability is the dominant objective.

Assets.Functionality: Internal register holding the 0..GPIO_NUM-1 output bits; written via bus writes to the output port and directly drives gpio_o. Controls the logic-levels driven to external pins.
Assets.Justification: Unauthorized modification of port_out (via a compromised bus/master) changes external output signals and can cause incorrect actuation or state corruption of attached devices. This is a classic integrity concern because the register controls externally-observable state.

Assets.Functionality: Synchronized capture of gpio_i that is used for bus read-back and as primary input to the IRQ evaluation logic.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or tampering of port_in (or its sampling timing) will change values observed by software and the IRQ logic, causing incorrect system responses. The primary risk is unauthorized modification of sampled data, so integrity is dominant.

Assets.Functionality: One-clock-old copy of port_in used to detect rising/falling edges in the IRQ trigger logic.
Assets.Justification: Altering or corrupting port_in2 changes edge-detection outcomes (false or missed edge detection), thereby changing interrupt behavior. This attacks correctness of event detection, so integrity is the main concern.

Assets.Functionality: Per-pin register selecting level vs. edge trigger mode; used together with irq_pol to compute irq_trig conditions.
Assets.Justification: If irq_typ is modified during operation, the kind of event detected (level vs. edge) changes and interrupts may trigger incorrectly or not at all. This is a configuration-integrity issue that affects correctness of IRQ detection.

Assets.Functionality: Per-pin register selecting polarity (high/low for level or rising/falling for edge) used in computing irq_trig conditions.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with irq_pol flips the meaning of input events (e.g., rising vs. falling), causing incorrect interrupt signaling. This is a configuration integrity risk as it directly changes event detection semantics.

Assets.Functionality: Per-pin enable bits that gate whether a detected trigger can set the pending interrupt (irq_pend).
Assets.Justification: Changing irq_en can enable or disable interrupt delivery for pins; unauthorized modification alters which events are allowed to produce pending interrupts, corrupting expected control-flow and behavior. This is primarily an integrity concern over interrupt configuration.

Assets.Functionality: Latched per-pin pending-interrupt bits that buffer irq_trig events (subject to irq_en and irq_clrn) until cleared; reduced to produce cpu_irq_o when any bit is set.
Assets.Justification: Manipulation of irq_pend (or its improper clearing) directly affects whether interrupts are reported to the CPU; clearing or preventing pending bits denies notification of events. The main impact is loss of interrupt availability to the CPU.

Assets.Functionality: Output signal that enables/disables the external clock generator used as the timer tick source; directly driven from the timer enable control bit.
Assets.Justification: If this output is forced inactive or otherwise prevented from enabling the external clock generator, the timer will not receive tick pulses and cannot operate, causing a denial-of-service of timer functionality. At integration level an attacker or misconfiguration of the connected clock generator controlled by this signal can therefore block the module's operation.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt request output driven when the internal interrupt-pending flag is set due to a counter-threshold match; used to notify the CPU or other masters of timer events.
Assets.Justification: If the interrupt output is blocked, masked or forced to an inactive state by external manipulation, the CPU will not be notified of timer events and higher-level operations depending on those interrupts will be disrupted. This represents a denial-of-service at integration level even though the timer core might still count internally.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit internal control register that holds the global enable bit and the three prescaler select bits which determine timer enable state and which clkgen_i bit is sampled as the tick.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or unauthorized modification of these control bits (enable or prescaler) will change the timer's operating mode, tick rate or disable it, producing incorrect timing behavior. Ensuring these bits are not tampered with is necessary to maintain correct and expected timer operation.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit internal threshold value loaded via bus writes; compared against the counter to produce a match event and generate the interrupt.
Assets.Justification: If the threshold value is modified unexpectedly (e.g., during operation) the time at which a match/interrupt occurs will be incorrect, leading to corrupted timing semantics for any software depending on the timer. Thus the integrity of the threshold register must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit internal counter that increments on each timer.tick while enabled and resets on match or when the timer is disabled; readable by the bus.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the counter value (or corrupting the mechanism that updates it) will change when a match occurs and break timing correctness; maintaining counter integrity is required to ensure the timer produces expected events. Although the counter is read-only from the bus, its internal value is central to correct operation and thus an integrity-critical state.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag set when a counter-threshold match occurs (while enabled) and cleared by irq_clr or when disabled; drives irq_o.
Assets.Justification: If the pending flag is suppressed or repeatedly cleared, interrupts will not be presented to the CPU even though matches may occur, causing a denial-of-service of the interrupt mechanism. Protecting the availability of the pending indication is necessary for timely delivery of timer events.

Assets.Functionality: Write-strobe signal asserted by bus writes to the control register's IRQ-clear bit; when asserted it clears the irq_pnd flag in the interrupt generator.
Assets.Justification: An attacker or buggy master that can repeatedly assert/force this strobe could continuously clear pending interrupts, preventing the CPU from ever observing them and causing a denial-of-service. Therefore control over this clear signal impacts the availability of the interrupt service.

Assets.Functionality: lock_q is a 32-bit vector holding the state of each hardware spinlock (one bit per lock). Bits are set on a claim (read transaction) and cleared on a release (write transaction); the vector is also returned (partially or fully) on read responses.
Assets.Justification: lock_q encodes critical control state that determines ownership of shared resources. Unauthorized or unintended modification of these bits (e.g., flipped or stuck bits) can grant or deny access to resources, corrupting system behavior and enabling escalation or denial-of-service, so integrity of lock_q is essential.

Assets.Functionality: sel is a one-hot 32-bit selection vector derived from the incoming bus address that indicates which individual lock index is targeted by the current bus request; it gates updates to lock_q and is ANDed with lock_q to form per-lock read responses.
Assets.Justification: sel is the control signal that determines which lock bit may be modified or observed. Tampering with sel (selecting the wrong index or suppressing the intended index) can cause incorrect lock modifications or reads, corrupting ownership semantics and enabling incorrect resource access, so integrity of sel is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Asynchronous single-wire serial data line that the serial TX engine toggles to transmit timed pulses (bits and reset) to WS281x smart LEDs.
Assets.Justification: neoled_o carries the actual LED payload; any unauthorized modification of the signal (timing or level) changes the transmitted bits and thus corrupts LED colors/behavior. Protecting this line against tampering is primarily an integrity concern because it directly affects correctness of output data.

Assets.Functionality: Selects whether FIFO words are sent as 24-bit RGB (mode='0') or 32-bit RGBW (mode='1'), affecting bit count and sreg indexing during transmission.
Assets.Justification: Corrupting ctrl.mode changes how many bits are transmitted and which bits are selected from the shift register, likely producing incorrect colors or mis-framed data. This directly alters the correctness of transmitted payloads, making integrity the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: When set, marks a FIFO write as a RESET (STROBE) command instead of normal LED color data; the serial engine uses this to enter the STROBE state.
Assets.Justification: A malicious modification of ctrl.strobe can convert intended data into RESETs or vice versa, changing transmitted behavior (e.g., sending unintended resets). This corrupts the intended data-flow and thus is primarily an integrity risk.

Assets.Functionality: 3-bit index into clkgen_i that selects which external pulse clock is sampled as pulse_clk for the serial timing engine.
Assets.Justification: Altering ctrl.clk_prsc changes the pulse_clk source and therefore the timing granularity used for pulse widths; incorrect selection can corrupt symbol timing and transmitted bits (wrong T_high/T_total cadence), impacting correctness of the protocol.

Assets.Functionality: 5-bit field specifying the total number of pulse-clock ticks that define a single symbol period (T_total) for bit transmission timing.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with ctrl.t_total modifies the duration of symbol periods and can violate the WS281x timing requirements, causing transmitted pulses to be misinterpreted by LEDs and corrupting data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Output that enables/disables the external clock generator used to derive the pulse_clk inputs for the serial TX engine.
Assets.Justification: If clkgen_en_o is disabled (or driven incorrectly), the serial engine will not receive the required pulse_clk and cannot perform transmissions, effectively denying LED functionality. Therefore the dominant risk is availability: manipulation can stop the module from operating.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt request output asserted according to FIFO status and ctrl.irq_conf to notify the CPU about FIFO empty/low conditions when the module is enabled.
Assets.Justification: irq_o is used to prompt the CPU to refill the FIFO or react to buffer state; if interrupts are suppressed or spuriously asserted, the CPU may not service the FIFO or may be overwhelmed, leading to loss of regular LED updates (denial-of-service). Protecting correct assertion of irq_o is therefore primarily an availability concern.

Assets.Functionality: Control bit that gates module operation: enables/disables the serial FSM, drives clkgen_en_o, and influences FIFO clearing via tx_fifo.clear.
Assets.Justification: Toggling ctrl.enable directly enables or disables the entire transmission engine and clears the FIFO; unauthorized changes can stop all LED transmissions or clear buffered data, producing a clear denial-of-service on the peripheral.

Assets.Functionality: Synchronous, high-active FIFO clear input that flushes/clears the TX FIFO; it is driven by the inverse of ctrl.enable so the FIFO is cleared when the module is disabled.
Assets.Justification: Forcing tx_fifo.clear causes loss of buffered data and prevents pending transmissions, effectively denying service. Preventing unauthorized assertions of this clear signal is primarily an availability concern.

Assets.Functionality: Status signal indicating that FIFO data is available (non-empty); used by the serial engine to begin transmission and by bus/status reads and IRQ logic to reflect FIFO state.
Assets.Justification: If tx_fifo.avail is manipulated (false negatives/positives), the serial engine or bus status logic may stall or misbehave, preventing regular refills and causing interruptions in LED updates. The dominant risk is loss of service (availability).

Assets.Functionality: Physical 1‑Wire line sense input sampled (synchronized into serial.wire_in) and used to read bits from devices and detect presence pulses on the 1‑Wire bus.
Assets.Justification: Manipulation of the sensed bus level directly changes the bits sampled by the serial engine and the presence detection result. An attacker controlling or spoofing this input can corrupt read data and presence detection, altering the integrity of reported device responses.

Assets.Functionality: Internal enable flag that turns the 1‑Wire controller and its clock generator usage on/off and forces the serial engine into reset/off when cleared.
Assets.Justification: Unexpected toggling of the enable bit during operations resets or disables the serial FSM and clears active behavior, corrupting command execution and transaction semantics. Integrity of operation depends on enable remaining correct during critical sequences.

Assets.Functionality: Flag sampled during RESET state indicating whether any device pulled the bus low (presence detected); gets combined into RX FIFO results.
Assets.Justification: Altering the presence flag yields an incorrect indication of device presence to the host, which can lead to wrong control decisions. The integrity of presence reporting is required for correct device enumeration and operation.

Assets.Functionality: Driver control for the 1‑Wire line; the serial engine drives this output to actively pull the line low (onewire_o='0') or release it/tristate (onewire_o='1') to generate bit time slots and reset pulses.
Assets.Justification: If the line driver is forced or disabled, the module cannot generate correct time slots or reset pulses, preventing any meaningful communication on the 1‑Wire bus. This directly enables a denial‑of‑service condition at integration level by blocking all transactions.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt output asserted when the module is enabled, TX FIFO empty and serial engine idle; signals transfer completion/ready state to the CPU.
Assets.Justification: If the interrupt line is suppressed or spoofed, the host may not be notified of completed transfers or may be misled, disrupting normal workflows. Availability of timely notifications is required for correct higher‑level operation, so compromising irq_o can deny correct service or cause misses.

Assets.Functionality: Output enable for the SoC clock generator; when asserted by ctrl.enable the external clock generator is allowed to run and provide clkgen_i sources used by the module.
Assets.Justification: If the clock generator enable is prevented from asserting, the selected clkgen_i source(s) may be unavailable so the module's base tick (clk_tick) never occurs. This prevents timed serial operations and results in a denial‑of‑service of the 1‑Wire controller.

Assets.Functionality: Provides the selectable clock inputs used by the internal clock generator (lowest 4 bits are used) to produce the base tick (t_base) for timing 1‑Wire operations.
Assets.Justification: An attacker changing the selected clock source or its values alters the base tick timing, breaking protocol timing windows and leading to incorrect sampling/drive behavior and corrupted transactions; therefore timing configuration must maintain integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Completion indicator asserted by the serial FSM when an operation finishes; used to write results into RX FIFO and to move the FSM to IDLE.
Assets.Justification: If completion is not asserted when operations finish or is falsely asserted, the RX FIFO won't be updated or operations may be prematurely considered complete, stalling or disrupting higher‑level flows. Correct availability of results depends on serial.done.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit configuration that enables or disables the channel; when '0' it clears counters, disables PWM activity and controls the per-channel clock generator request (clkgen_en_o).
Assets.Justification: cfg_en determines whether the channel is active and affects counters and clk requests; unauthorized changes during operation will alter channel behavior (enable/disable) and produce incorrect outputs or timing.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit duty-cycle setting that defines the compare threshold for the duty counter and therefore the high/low ratio of the PWM waveform for the channel.
Assets.Justification: cfg_duty directly controls the output duty of the PWM. Corrupting this value changes the physical output ratio (e.g., motor speed or LED brightness), so it must be protected from unauthorized modification.

Assets.Functionality: 10-bit fine divider compared against the internal cnt_cdiv to generate a single-cycle cnt_tick that advances the duty counter and sets PWM timing resolution.
Assets.Justification: cfg_cdiv controls the fine timing granularity of PWM periods. Tampering with cfg_cdiv will change tick generation and thus the effective PWM frequency/period, leading to incorrect timing behavior.

Assets.Functionality: 3-bit index selecting one bit of clkgen_i as the pre-scaled clock source used to step the fine divider, thereby coarsely selecting the channel clock speed.
Assets.Justification: cfg_prsc chooses which clkgen_i bit drives the fine divider. Malicious or erroneous changes alter which clock source the channel uses and will corrupt PWM frequency selection and behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Carries the 32-bit configuration word that is decoded into the channel configuration registers (cfg_*).
Assets.Justification: wdata_i directly determines all configuration fields for a channel on a write. Malicious or erroneous modifications to this input will corrupt channel configuration (enable, prescaler, polarity, divider, duty) and thus alter or break PWM behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Per-channel internal write-enable bits computed from bus address and bus transaction signals; forwarded to each channel's we_i to gate register writes.
Assets.Justification: we controls whether channel configuration registers are updated. Manipulating these bits (or the logic that generates them) can cause unauthorized writes to channel registers or prevent intended writes, corrupting configuration state and PWM behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Enables latching of wdata_i into the channel configuration registers on a clock edge; gates when configuration changes occur.
Assets.Justification: we_i governs when configuration words are committed; if asserted or suppressed incorrectly, cfg_en/prsc/pol/cdiv/duty can be overwritten or left stale, producing unintended output timing or polarity and silently corrupting the channel’s programmed behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Multi-bit output carrying the per-channel PWM signals (up to 16 channels) to downstream logic or external pins.
Assets.Justification: pwm_o is the module's functional output; if it becomes unavailable (blocked, forced static or otherwise prevented from toggling) the PWM signals cannot perform their intended control tasks. Loss of this output equates to denial-of-service for devices depending on PWM.

Assets.Functionality: Provides the prescaled/coarse clock bits that channels index into using cfg_prsc to produce fine-tuned cnt_tick pulses driving PWM timing.
Assets.Justification: clkgen_i selects the coarse timing source for channels via cfg_prsc. If clkgen_i is manipulated, the derived cnt_tick timing changes and channel frequencies/duty timing are corrupted, impacting correct PWM operation.

Assets.Functionality: Vector of per-channel clkgen_en_o signals (ce(i)) from instances; these are ORed to form the module-level clkgen_en_o request.
Assets.Justification: If the ce vector is suppressed such that no channel can request the global clock generator, the module-level clkgen_en_o will remain deasserted and PWM channels cannot progress — causing denial of service. Therefore availability of the aggregated per-channel clock requests is critical to overall operation.

Assets.Functionality: OR-reduced per-channel enable requests indicating whether the global clock generator must be enabled for any active channel.
Assets.Justification: clkgen_en_o is used by integration to enable the shared clock generator; if this enable is not honored or is driven wrong, channels will not receive pre-scaled clock ticks and PWM outputs will cease toggling, causing a denial-of-service of PWM functionality.

Assets.Functionality: Active-low chip-select for the SDI link; synchronized into sync.csn and used to start/abort transmissions and reported in the control status bit (ctrl_cs_active).
Assets.Justification: If sdi_csn_i is not asserted (or is held inactive), no transfers will start; if it is spuriously toggled the serial engine aborts transfers. Thus unavailability or manipulation of this signal can directly deny SDI data-transfer functionality.

Assets.Functionality: Asynchronous serial data input synchronized into sync.sdi and sampled into serial.sdi_ff then shifted into serial.sreg and finally written to the RX FIFO on serial.done.
Assets.Justification: Tampering or injection on sdi_dat_i directly modifies received payload bits, corrupting received data content. The dominant concern is integrity because altered input bits change the semantic data delivered to the CPU.

Assets.Functionality: MSB of the serial shift register (serial.sreg) driven out as the serial transmit bitstream for the remote device; reflects the next transmit bit (TX) from the FIFO or zeros when empty.
Assets.Justification: sdi_dat_o conveys the module's transmitted bits; corruption of the transmit path or of the driving register changes what is sent to the external host. The primary risk is integrity of the transmitted data.

Assets.Functionality: Asserts an interrupt to the CPU when the peripheral is enabled and configured FIFO/status conditions (RX/TX available, half/full, etc.) match enabled IRQ control bits.
Assets.Justification: If irq_o is blocked or prevented from asserting, the CPU may not be notified of RX/TX conditions, causing missed servicing or stalled data processing. This is primarily an availability concern (loss of service/notification).

Assets.Functionality: Control bit written by the CPU to enable/disable the SDI; when '0' it causes tx_fifo and rx_fifo to be cleared and disables the serial engine (serial.state bit2 used).
Assets.Justification: When ctrl.enable is deasserted the engine is disabled and FIFOs are cleared, preventing normal operation; unauthorized clearing or disabling effectively creates a denial of service, making availability the dominant objective.

Assets.Functionality: Synchronized and debounced chip-select used internally to detect start and abort of transmissions (derived from sdi_csn_i).
Assets.Justification: sync.csn is the internal gating signal for transfer start/abort; if it is absent or wrong inside the logic, transfers cannot be started or will be aborted, leading to denial of service. Availability is the primary impact.

Assets.Functionality: Internal derived edge-detect signal (XOR of clock history) used to step the serial FSM on detected clock edges.
Assets.Justification: Loss or corruption of sync.sck prevents the FSM from advancing through bit phases; without proper edge detection, the serial engine cannot operate, producing a denial of service.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit shift register loaded from tx_fifo.rdata (or zero) for transmission and shifted-in with sampled bits to produce received bytes that are written into the RX FIFO (rx_fifo.wdata). Its MSB drives sdi_dat_o.
Assets.Justification: serial.sreg directly holds TX bytes and assembled RX bytes; corruption of its contents alters data transmitted or delivered to the CPU, so integrity of this register is critical.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit incoming RX stream data which is written into the RX FIFO (rx_fifo.wdata[31:0]) when slink_rx_valid_i is asserted.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or injection of slink_rx_data_i directly alters the data stored in the RX FIFO and later consumed by the host, changing system behavior. The dominant concern is integrity since incorrect/forged payloads will corrupt application data flows.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit source/routing metadata packed into rx_fifo.wdata[35:32] and later restored to route_src on FIFO reads and reported to the host.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with slink_rx_src_i can cause mislabelling/misrouting of incoming data and mislead the host about origin or required handling. The primary risk is integrity corruption of routing metadata that affects downstream processing.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit 'last' flag written into rx_fifo.wdata[36] to indicate stream/packet termination and backed up to rx_last on FIFO read.
Assets.Justification: Altering the last flag changes stream boundaries interpretation (e.g., merging or splitting packets) and can corrupt higher-level protocol semantics; this is an integrity concern for the stream metadata.

Assets.Functionality: Output driven from rx_fifo.free to indicate free FIFO entries and whether the module can accept another RX beat.
Assets.Justification: If slink_rx_ready_o is forced or stuck, upstream components may be prevented from sending or misinformed, causing loss of service or deadlock; availability of the receive path is the primary risk.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit TX stream data driven from tx_fifo.rdata[31:0] when the TX FIFO has data and the downstream consumer reads it.
Assets.Justification: If the TX payload is corrupted (either from FIFO corruption or routing misconfiguration), consumers receive incorrect data; the main concern is integrity of transmitted payloads.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit destination metadata driven from tx_fifo.rdata[35:32] that selects the destination/route for the outgoing stream.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with tx destination bits causes misrouting of transmitted data (delivering to wrong consumer or bypassing checks), compromising correct system operation; integrity of routing metadata is the main risk.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates that TX FIFO has available data (driven by tx_fifo.avail) and qualifies the slink_tx_data_o/t dst/last outputs as valid for the downstream consumer.
Assets.Justification: If tx_valid_o is suppressed or stuck, downstream will not accept data and the transmission path is effectively denied; thus availability of TX service is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit 'last' signal for TX taken from tx_fifo.rdata[36] to signal packet/stream termination on outgoing interface.
Assets.Justification: Modifying the TX last bit changes stream/packet framing on the output, potentially corrupting protocol boundaries; this is an integrity issue for transmitted stream semantics.

Assets.Functionality: Input handshake from downstream indicating readiness; when asserted causes tx_fifo.re to pop the next TX entry and advance outputs.
Assets.Justification: If the ready line is prevented from asserting (or forced to assert inappropriately), the module can be stalled or forced to pop entries prematurely, causing denial-of-service or data-loss; availability is dominant.

Assets.Functionality: Asserted based on ctrl.enable and RX-side ctrl.irq_* settings combined with rx_fifo status (avail/half/free) to notify the host about RX events.
Assets.Justification: If interrupts are suppressed or spurious, the host may not be notified about received data or may be interrupted excessively causing service disruption; interrupt signaling primarily affects availability of event notification.

Assets.Functionality: Asserted based on ctrl.enable and TX-side ctrl.irq_* settings combined with tx_fifo status to notify the host about TX conditions (empty/not-half/not-full).
Assets.Justification: Manipulation of TX interrupt output impacts host responsiveness to transmit conditions (e.g., refilling FIFOs), enabling denial-of-service or missed transmissions; availability of transmit event signaling is the core concern.

Assets.Functionality: Global module enable flag from the CTRL register that gates operation; when '0' RX/TX FIFOs are cleared/inactive and interrupts are masked.
Assets.Justification: Changing ctrl.enable disables the module and clears FIFOs which results in loss of streaming functionality and data; the principal impact is denial-of-service to RX/TX services.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the destination routing value that is merged into TX FIFO write data (route_dst <= bus write) and thus used for subsequent TX entries.
Assets.Justification: If route_dst is modified improperly the module will send data to incorrect destinations or leak data to unintended recipients; integrity of routing configuration is the main concern.

Assets.Functionality: Backed-up source/routing information taken from the RX FIFO read data and returned in the routing read register for the host (route_src <= rx_fifo.rdata(35 downto 32)).
Assets.Justification: Corrupt route_src gives the host incorrect provenance information for received data and can lead to wrong processing or trust decisions; preserving correctness of source metadata is an integrity requirement.

Assets.Functionality: Serial data output (MOSI) driven from the transmit shift register (rtx_engine.sreg(7)) that sends bits to the selected SPI peripheral.
Assets.Justification: Altering the MOSI bitstream (or the logic that drives it) will corrupt transmitted payloads and thus corrupt integrator data/commands. The SPI controller is not a crypto primitive in this design, so integrity of outgoing data is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Serial data input sampled into the transceiver (synchronized into rtx_engine.sdi_sync) and shifted into the receive path and RX FIFO.
Assets.Justification: Injected or modified MISO bits can cause incorrect data to be presented to the host (via RX FIFO), corrupting system behavior or decisions. Since the module is not used for cryptography here, integrity of received data is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Up to 8 active-low chip-select outputs; the chip_select process asserts the selected CS low based on rtx_engine.cs_ctrl to enable a specific SPI peripheral for a transaction.
Assets.Justification: If CS outputs are forced, blocked, or mis-asserted at integration time, the controller cannot communicate with the intended peripheral (denial-of-service). While mis-assertion can also affect integrity, preventing access (availability) is the dominant risk for system operation.

Assets.Functionality: Output signal that enables an external pre-scaled clock generator when the SPI controller is enabled (driven from ctrl.enable).
Assets.Justification: If this enable is inhibited or deasserted at integration level, the SPI clock source may not run and no SPI transfers can occur, producing a denial-of-service for SPI communications.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt line asserted when enabled and configured FIFO/engine conditions (RX available, TX empty, TX not half full, or idle) occur to notify the host.
Assets.Justification: Suppressing or forging the IRQ can prevent the host from learning about transfer completion or FIFO conditions (DoS or missed events). The primary impact is availability of timely notifications to the integrator.

Assets.Asset Name: SPI Serial Clock Output - Availability of Transaction Timing
Assets.Functionality: SPI serial clock driven from the transceiver's sck (rtx_engine.sck) and controlled by clock generation logic (clock_generator) to time bit transfers according to CPOL/CPHA and divider settings.
Assets.Justification: spi_clk_o is required for active SPI transfers (used to clock both sampling and shifting). If the clock signal is unavailable, blocked, or held in an incorrect state at integration, SPI transactions cannot complete, causing denial of service for SPI communication — an availability issue.

Assets.Functionality: Control-register bit that gates the SPI engine, clock generation, and clears both FIFOs when deasserted (global enable for SPI operation).
Assets.Justification: Unauthorized modification of the enable bit directly disables the SPI engine and flushes FIFOs, resulting in a complete denial-of-service of SPI functionality; availability is therefore the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: 3-bit index selecting which pre-scaled clock in clkgen_i is used by the internal clock generator to produce SPI timing pulses.
Assets.Justification: Changing the prescaler at runtime affects bit timing and can cause mis-sampling or timing violations that corrupt data transfers; this makes integrity the dominant risk.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit fine divider value compared against internal counter to generate periodic spi_clk_en pulses that advance the transceiver state machine.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with cdiv alters the generated bit-rate/phase timing and can cause systematic data corruption; thus protecting correctness (integrity) of transfers is critical.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit shift register holding the current transmit byte (MSB output) and shifting in sampled MISO bits during transmission.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of the shift register contents or its shifting behavior directly modifies transmitted and received bytes, breaking data correctness; integrity protection is therefore required.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit control field from TX FIFO command entries; bit(3) indicates active and bits(2:0) select which CS line to assert for the next transaction.
Assets.Justification: If this internal control is altered, the controller can select the wrong peripheral or fail to assert CS, causing incorrect transactions or cross-device corruption; integrity of selection is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Vector of enable channels that is OR-reduced to produce the internal enable 'en'; when deasserted the internal counter is held at zero and no clock-enable pulses are generated.
Assets.Justification: This external input gates the generation of all derived clock-enable pulses. If an integrator or attacker can force or keep this input deasserted (or manipulate it), peripherals and logic relying on the generated clk_en_o pulses can be starved of timing ticks, producing a denial-of-service of downstream functionality.

Assets.Functionality: 12-bit counter that increments while 'en' is active; individual bit rises are used to generate the single-cycle clk_en_o pulses for various divided clocks.
Assets.Justification: The counter directly produces the timing transitions used to create the one-cycle clock-enable ticks; if the counter is corrupted, held, or otherwise prevented from toggling correctly, the derived pulses will be missing or incorrect and dependent logic can be denied service or operate incorrectly.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the processor clock frequency (32-bit) initialized from generic CLOCK_FREQUENCY and can be updated at runtime by bus write transactions to sysinfo word index 0; read by software via the bus response to determine system timing/configuration.
Assets.Justification: sysinfo(0) conveys critical configuration information (processor clock frequency) that software relies on for correct operation. The RTL explicitly permits bus writes to sysinfo(0), so an attacker who can modify or corrupt writes could change this value and cause incorrect timing assumptions or misconfiguration; therefore its integrity must be protected.

Assets.Functionality: Provides the 8-bit random data byte produced by the neoTRNG core (LFSR-style mixed/de-biased stream); pulses valid_o when the byte is new.
Assets.Justification: The random byte is consumed by cryptographic protocols and should not be observable via unintended paths; premature or unauthorized disclosure enables eavesdroppers to harvest entropy or correlate internal state, weakening protocol secrecy.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit output from the John von Neumann de-biasing stage which is fed into the LFSR-style sample shift-register to build the final random byte.
Assets.Justification: debias_data determines each contributed bit of the final random byte; corruption biases the distribution, degrades statistical quality, and reduces effective entropy, undermining cryptographic strength.

Assets.Functionality: Local sampled copy of the enable_i input that gates sampling; when low the sampler is restarted/cleared and when high sampling proceeds.
Assets.Justification: sample_en gates entropy collection; if stuck low the TRNG never produces bytes, and if stuck high when a restart is needed the pipeline can wedge or produce stale output—both conditions deny timely random data to consumers.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the TRNG enable bit written by the host control register and drives neoTRNG.enable_i; turning it on/off starts or restarts sampling and the entropy pipeline.
Assets.Justification: The enable bit controls when entropy generation starts or restarts; unauthorized or corrupted writes can silently disable the TRNG or cause unintended resets of the sampling pipeline, compromising correctness of operation and downstream assumptions.

Assets.Functionality: Write-only flag driven by the host that triggers a synchronous clear of the data FIFO (auto-clears next cycle); used to erase the FIFO contents.
Assets.Justification: fifo_clr erases buffered random bytes; spurious assertion discards valid entropy and breaks sequencing, while suppression leaves stale data present for reads—both corrupt the intended stream semantics.

Assets.Functionality: Status flag from the FIFO indicating whether valid data is available for host reads; exposed to software via the control register available bit.
Assets.Justification: If the availability flag is manipulated (reported false when data exists) the host may refrain from reading the DATA register and be denied entropy; falsified availability information therefore enables a practical DoS on consumers relying on that status.

Assets.Functionality: Flag from the FIFO that indicates whether there is at least one free entry to accept a new random byte written by the neoTRNG.
Assets.Justification: fifo.free governs admission of new bytes; a false negative stalls writes and starves consumers, while a false positive can cause overflow/overwrite and lost data—both reduce the availability of usable entropy.

Assets.Functionality: Read-enable signal asserted when the bus performs a read of the data register, causing the FIFO to pop the next byte for the host.
Assets.Justification: If reads are suppressed or the read gate is prevented from asserting, the host cannot retrieve available random bytes even if they exist in the FIFO, producing a denial-of-service at the integration level for consumers of TRNG data.

Assets.Functionality: On-chip FIFO (the 'random pool') that stores generated random bytes from neoTRNG until the host reads them via the bus interface; it exposes rdata to the bus read path and accepts wdata from the neoTRNG core.
Assets.Justification: The FIFO contents are the stored entropy delivered to consumers; unauthorized modification or corruption (e.g. unexpected writes, silent corruption) changes the values read by the host and breaks the integrity of the random data stream. Ensuring FIFO contents are not tampered with is necessary to guarantee correctness of delivered randomness.

Assets.Functionality: Software-writable enable bit for the TWD module; also drives clkgen_en_o to enable the SoC clock generator used for input sampling and effectively gates major functionality of the peripheral.
Assets.Justification: If this signal is deasserted the entire TWD controller becomes non-operational (FIFOs cleared and sampling stopped), which is a direct denial-of-service to I2C device functionality. Protecting availability of this control is therefore essential to keep the peripheral usable.

Assets.Functionality: Output that enables the external clock generator used to produce the sample clocks for SDA/SCL filtering and sampling.
Assets.Justification: If clkgen_en_o is deasserted or the external clock generator is prevented from providing the sample clock, the module cannot obtain filtered samples of SDA/SCL and will not be able to perform transactions, producing a DoS at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: External serial data line input sampled and synchronized to detect bus levels, start/stop conditions and to capture incoming bits from a host/master.
Assets.Justification: If the SDA input is driven, held, or otherwise made unavailable/unreliable at integration, the controller cannot correctly receive bytes or detect bus events, preventing normal device operation (DoS). The input is therefore availability-critical.

Assets.Functionality: Physical SCL input sampled and synchronized to detect edges used for timing sampling, byte framing, and start/stop detection.
Assets.Justification: If SCL is not provided or is interfered with at integration, the controller cannot sample bits or detect framing, which prevents transaction progress and results in a denial-of-service for I2C communication.

Assets.Functionality: Open-drain SDA output driven by the bus engine to transmit data bits and to send ACK/NACK (default released/high).
Assets.Justification: This output directly determines bits placed on the I2C bus (ACK/NACK and data). Unauthorized modification of its value or timing corrupts the protocol and transmitted data, so the integrity of twd_sda_o must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: Supplies the byte to be transmitted on the bus: either TX FIFO output, tx_dummy (if enabled), or default ones when empty; used to initialize engine.sreg for bitwise transmission.
Assets.Justification: This signal is the immediate source of bits driven on SDA for READ transfers; corruption or unintended modification results in incorrect data being presented to the I2C master, directly violating data integrity. It must therefore be integrity-protected.

Assets.Functionality: Output pin state used to represent controller-driven SCL state (default released/high); used to implement open-drain behavior or indicate controller-driven SCL.
Assets.Justification: The output can affect bus timing and transaction sequencing; unexpected modification of twd_scl_o can corrupt sampling/transfer timing and thus corrupt the integrity of exchanged data and protocol sequencing.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt line asserted when enabled control flags and FIFO/status conditions indicate an interrupt-worthy event (RX available, RX full, TX empty).
Assets.Justification: If irq_o is suppressed or made unavailable, the CPU or integrator may not be notified of received data or FIFO conditions, preventing timely processing and effectively causing degraded or denied operation at the system level.

Assets.Functionality: Backup of the last transmitted TX byte used as fallback transmission when the TX FIFO is empty and tx_dummy_en is enabled.
Assets.Justification: When tx_dummy_en is active the engine may transmit this stored byte instead of FIFO content; misuse or unexpected selection of tx_dummy changes transmitted data (replay of previous byte), impacting integrity of read responses.

Assets.Functionality: Global module enable bit that gates the TWI unit operation, drives engine.state(2), controls clock-generator reset behavior and the clkgen_en_o output.
Assets.Justification: ctrl.enable gates the entire operational capability of the TWI block: clearing FIFOs and stopping the engine when deasserted. If an attacker or faulty integrator toggles this signal during runtime, the TWI service can be denied (DoS) by repeatedly disabling or clearing the module.

Assets.Functionality: Selects which bit of the external pre-scaled clock vector (clkgen_i) is sampled to produce the internal clk_gen.tick timing used by the phase generator and engine.
Assets.Justification: ctrl.prsc defines the effective SCL base rate; corruption changes the bit period and violates I²C timing, causing framing errors or out-of-spec transactions, so its value must be trustworthy.

Assets.Functionality: Fine-grained clock divider value used by the internal clock generator to determine when to assert clk_gen.tick (counts up to ctrl.cdiv).
Assets.Justification: ctrl.cdiv shapes tick generation and duty/hold timing; if altered, setup/hold windows and SCL high/low durations become incorrect, corrupting transfers even when logic otherwise behaves.

Assets.Functionality: Pulse asserted when a byte transmission/reception completes; used to write RX FIFO and to transition engine state back to IDLE.
Assets.Justification: engine.done delineates byte boundaries and triggers FIFO updates; spurious or missing pulses cause duplicated/dropped bytes and incorrect state transitions, corrupting the data stream.

Assets.Functionality: External serial data input sampled and synchronized into io_con.sda_in_ff for bus sensing and as the sampled input during transmissions.
Assets.Justification: twi_sda_i is the truth source for received bits and ACK/NACK; corruption or mis-sampling yields wrong data and protocol markers, leading to silent data corruption or failed transactions.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level SDA drive signal reflecting io_con.sda_out; actively drives SDA low to claim the bus and releases it to let the pull-up drive it high.
Assets.Justification: Incorrect SDA drive level or timing produces invalid start/stop edges or bit values and can break arbitration, corrupting transactions for all devices on the bus.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates that a bus operation is currently in progress (derived from engine.state); used by status reads and IRQ generation.
Assets.Justification: If engine.busy is stuck high, software defers new operations indefinitely; if stuck low, overlapping requests can be issued that the engine cannot serialize, causing stalls or retries—both harm forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: External SCL input sampled and synchronized to detect bus state and clock-stretching conditions via io_con.scl_in_ff.
Assets.Justification: twi_scl_i is required to detect clock stretching and phase completion; if not sensed correctly, the controller may wait forever or advance prematurely, wedging the bus and degrading availability.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level SCL drive signal reflecting io_con.scl_out; used by the engine/clock generator to actively control the SCL line during phases.
Assets.Justification: If SCL cannot be driven/released at the right times, bit phases cannot progress and transfers stall or deadlock, directly impacting bus availability.

Assets.Functionality: Output reflecting ctrl.enable used to enable an external pre-scaler/clock source; exposes the module enable state to external clocking logic.
Assets.Justification: clkgen_en_o controls the external prescaler; if not asserted when needed, the internal tick never occurs and the engine cannot progress, while spurious assertion can disturb shared clocking—both reduce availability.

Assets.Functionality: Signals the host that the TWI module is enabled and ready/idle (TX FIFO empty and engine idle); used by the host to schedule further actions.
Assets.Justification: If irq_o is suppressed, the host may not service the peripheral promptly, leading to idle time and stalled workflows; if asserted spuriously, it can trigger interrupt storms that starve normal processing—both harm overall availability.

Assets.Functionality: Output that enables/gates the external clock generator feeding the UART; driven directly from uart enable control to start/stop UART clocking.
Assets.Justification: If clkgen_en_o is de-asserted or prevented from enabling the external clock, the UART will not receive its baud timing and thus cannot operate, causing a denial-of-service. This signal therefore dominates availability risk at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: Asynchronous serial TX output driven by the transmitter shift register to send serial bits to external devices.
Assets.Justification: If the TX line is forced, shorted, or otherwise made unavailable at integration, the module cannot deliver transmitted data, resulting in service loss. While it carries application data, the primary integration-level risk is preventing transmissions (DoS).

Assets.Functionality: Asynchronous serial RX input sampled and synchronized by the receiver FSM to capture incoming serial bytes.
Assets.Justification: An attacker who injects or tampers with uart_rxd_i can modify the received byte-stream and thereby corrupt data delivered to the system, changing program behavior or data content. The dominant concern is integrity of the incoming data flow.

Assets.Functionality: Active-low RTS output indicating whether the UART is ready to receive; controlled by FIFO fill levels and hw flow-control enable.
Assets.Justification: If uart_rtsn_o is manipulated or driven to indicate 'not ready', a connected peer will stop sending data, preventing reception and causing a denial-of-service. Therefore this signal primarily impacts availability at integration.

Assets.Functionality: Active-low CTS input sampled for transmitter enable decisions; prevents the transmitter from starting new frames when de-asserted and hw flow-control is enabled.
Assets.Justification: If uart_ctsn_i is forced to disallow transmissions, the UART transmitter will be prevented from sending, creating a DoS on outbound communication. The principal integration-level risk is loss of service.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt line asserted based on RX FIFO thresholds (not-empty, half-full, full) when enabled to notify CPU of receive events.
Assets.Justification: Suppressing or spurious assertion of irq_rx_o can prevent the CPU from being informed of received data (or flood it), effectively denying timely processing of incoming bytes. The dominant threat is interruption/denial of normal RX handling (availability).

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt line asserted based on TX FIFO thresholds (empty, not-half-full) when enabled to notify CPU about transmit-space conditions.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with irq_tx_o can prevent the CPU from knowing when it can enqueue more data or can create spurious conditions, disrupting transmission scheduling. This primarily impacts availability of transmit service.

Assets.Asset Name: RX FIFO Read Data (dequeued receive byte)
Assets.Functionality: 8-bit data read from the RX FIFO and presented to the bus during data-register read accesses.
Assets.Justification: If rx_fifo.rdata is corrupted before readback, the system receives incorrect byte values, altering program state or data processing outcomes. The dominant security risk is integrity of the received data presented to the CPU.

Assets.Functionality: Control bit that globally enables or disables UART operation; gates transmitter, receiver and related logic and also drives clkgen_en_o.
Assets.Justification: Changing ctrl.enable will enable/disable the entire UART; disabling it makes the module non-functional and prevents all serial I/O. At integration level, this is the dominant availability control point for the peripheral.

Assets.Functionality: 10-bit baud divisor reloaded into per-bit counters to set the bit timing for transmitter and receiver.
Assets.Justification: If ctrl.baud is modified, the transmitter/receiver timing will change and cause corrupted communication (mismatched bit sampling), altering the correctness of exchanged bytes. This is a configuration that directly impacts data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 3-bit prescaler selecting which bit of the clkgen_i vector is used as uart_clk (affects effective baud timing).
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the prescaler will alter uart_clk selection and thus change bit timing, which can corrupt transmissions and receptions. The primary risk is integrity degradation of serial data due to incorrect timing.

Assets.Functionality: Status flag indicating an RX FIFO overrun (set when a write happens while fifo.free = '0'); exposed via control read status and used to detect lost incoming data.
Assets.Justification: rx_engine.over signals that incoming data was dropped due to a full FIFO; if suppressed, software cannot detect/recover from loss and the interface silently desynchronizes, while if stuck high it forces unnecessary clears/back-pressure, throttling throughput—both degrading availability.

Assets.Functionality: Output that enables the external clock generator/prescaler when the WDT is enabled; gates the timing source (prsc_tick) used to start and advance the watchdog counter.
Assets.Justification: If clkgen_en_o is prevented from asserting or is driven incorrectly at integration, the prescaler/tick will not be provided and the watchdog counter will not progress, disabling the WDT functionality and preventing the module from performing its recovery/reset role (Denial-of-service on WDT).

Assets.Functionality: Control bit that enables or disables the watchdog: starting the timeout counter and enabling the clock-generator output when set, and clearing the counter when cleared.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with ctrl.enable (clearing or preventing it from being set) will stop the watchdog from starting/counting and thereby prevent the WDT from performing system recovery, causing a loss of the module's intended availability/safety function.

Assets.Functionality: Lock bit that prevents further writes to the control register when set; attempted writes to a locked CTRL register result in a forced indication (reset_force) and, in strict mode, can cause a reset.
Assets.Justification: ctrl.lock protects the integrity of the WDT configuration; if the lock bit is maliciously cleared or prevented from being set, an attacker (or faulty integration) can alter critical configuration such as timeout or strict behavior, corrupting intended behavior and security policy.

Assets.Functionality: Configuration bit that, when set, enforces strict behavior: illegal accesses (wrong password or writes to locked config) cause a hardware reset instead of being ignored.
Assets.Justification: Altering ctrl.strict changes how the module reacts to illegal accesses; changing this bit undermines the integrity of the WDT's enforcement policy (either enabling unexpected resets or suppressing required resets), thus impacting correct security semantics.

Assets.Functionality: 24-bit programmed timeout compare value stored in the control register; compared against the internal counter to detect a watchdog timeout event.
Assets.Justification: If ctrl.timeout is modified illegitimately, the timing window for watchdog expiration is corrupted (too short or too long), directly changing system behavior and breaking the integrity of the safety policy the WDT is supposed to enforce.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit register that records the cause of the last system reset (external, debugger, watchdog timeout, or invalid watchdog access) for software readback.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with reset_cause can mislead software about the origin of the last reset, causing incorrect decisions in higher-level fault handling or diagnostics; maintaining the integrity of this status information is important for correct system behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Regular tick signal derived from the external clock-generator input (clkgen_i) that drives the watchdog counter at defined intervals.
Assets.Justification: If prsc_tick is missing, suppressed, or generated incorrectly, the watchdog counter will fail to advance as intended. This can prevent expected timeouts or trigger spurious ones, undermining the watchdog’s availability and reliable operation.

Assets.Functionality: 24-bit internal timeout counter that increments on prescaler ticks while the watchdog is active and is reset when the watchdog is fed or disabled.
Assets.Justification: cnt enforces the watchdog’s liveness window; if it is stalled or cleared incorrectly the watchdog may never expire (hung systems persist), while premature or accelerated counting triggers spurious timeouts and resets—both conditions disrupt forward progress and service availability.

Assets.Functionality: Signal asserted when the running counter equals the programmed timeout while counting, indicating that a watchdog timeout condition has occurred.
Assets.Justification: cnt_timeout initiates the watchdog’s fault response; if suppressed when the threshold is reached, hung software is never recovered, and if asserted spuriously it forces unnecessary resets—either outcome degrades system availability.
